book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: TLDR: It's a good book for folks who like a gentle, memory-intensive approach to attachment; it just didn't work for me. This is a good introduction to attachment theory. I read it cover to cover, and did many of the exercises. Unfortunately, a large part of the book wasn't very helpful for me. Most of the exercises rely on "remember a time when." If you're the sort of person who has memory issues or who doesn't respond to the remember-when approach, this just stops everything dead in its tracks. I'd have preferred more issue-identifying and forward-thinking exercises. And while examples from the writer's practice are ok, I'd have also liked a bit more academic meat in there regarding data/studies.

Multe cărți m-au ajutat să îmbunătățesc aspecte ale vieții mele, însă în ceea ce privește relațiile interpersonale, aceasta a fost cu adevărat revelatoare. Very well put together. Each type of style has it's own section after the section where you identify which style you are. So far I have found this book to be very helpful.

review_body: Very helpful in understanding the various attachment styles and what is most important to a relationship: consent, safety and security. It also invites us to understand our partners more empathetically and implement rituals of kindness, give and take, appreciation, affection, openness, playfulness, commitment, and joy.

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: Amazing book and amazing model for relationship security. Indeed all problems and relationships come from insecurity and this book and the attachment theory in general provides tools to become more secure in yourself and to practice the behavior of security so you can have all that you want in relationships. That's what I got out of it and attachment theory so far.

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: This book was HARD to read. Not because it was complicated or complex and not because it dense; simply because it asks you to look deep within yourself and figure out why you do the things you do in relationships and why you view things the way you do. It asks extremely hard questions about your most important relationships and why they turned out the way they did. It has chapters covering each of the attachment styles and a lot of workbook exercises to do to help you understand yourself better and to help you try and work through any issues you might have. The final chapters cover what it looks like to be in relationships with people who have different styles than you and then how to improve your attachment style. It gives you both personal exercises to work on and relationship exercises that you can work on with your partner to help you both understand each other better. This book opened my eyes about so many miscommunications I’ve had in my relationships with friends, family, and romantic partners. I highly recommend this book to anyone who has found that they’ve had issues in relationships, even if it’s not you that has trouble communicating, it has a lot of information about how to be with people who have trouble communicating.

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: This is a decent beginner book to attachment theory. I definitely felt seen when they described anxious attachment, and there were a few suggestions I will keep in mind when dealing with the people in my life who are more avoidant. Overall, though, I wished there had been more concrete instructions on what the right way to deal with problems were. A lot of the exercises seemed rather silly and/or not super helpful as I have a hard time imagining past scenarios when books ask me to. I am definitely going to be finding a more in-depth version of this topic to read next, but I don't regret the time reading this one.

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: The Attachment Theory Workbook is a solid means of examining yourself and your relation to others. Equal parts theory and exercise, by the conclusion of this book you will have a solid understanding of your attachment type, the attachment type of those with whom you regularly relate, and how to use this knowledge to improve yourself and your key relationships. The work within The Attachment Theory Workbook is not easy, and herein lies the power of this experience. This workbook will inspire you to take a close, honest look at yourself and your relationships, which is no easy task, yet highly rewarding when all is said and done. An effective method for progressing through this book is to read a section of theory until you reach an exercise and then complete the exercise. If you do this amount of minimum work daily, you will progress through the workbook at a regular and achievable pace. The Attachment Theory Workbook is perfect for those who enjoy self improvement and are seeking to optimize their experience and relationships within their daily life.

I think that’s why I bought the workbook, I wanted to do activities that were directly linked to my attachment style. I really enjoyed also being able to read and learn about the other attachment styles. It definitely made a difference in how I viewed past relationships. I will say that this book is good for couples who live together. It doesn’t give any advice for anyone in a long distance relationship or anyone who’s polyamorous.

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: A nice cute beginner’s book to the attachment styles. The book is super short and covers all of the styles, so naturally it doesn’t go too deep and could probably be more informative. Still, it did give me more perspective than I may have gotten from watching multiple one-minute long videos. I really enjoyed the small relationship dynamic examples that they gave. They really helped to fully explain some of the concepts. I also really liked that they were not all romantic examples. I do wish that the workbook had more techniques to move from an insecure to a more secure style. For example, it says many times that anxious attachments need to work on self-soothing, obviously. However, IT doesn’t give ways to do so. Instead, it just allows the reader to write out their own ideas themselves. Still, great place to start.

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: O stylach przywiązania w dedykowanej im książce, która oferuje coś więcej niż tylko podstawową charakterystykę znaną z innych publikacji. Jej największym atutem jest wyraźnie praktyczne, „robocze” podejście – nie zatrzymuje się na teorii, lecz prowadzi krok dalej, w stronę realnej pracy nad sobą. Mnóstwo ankiet, zadań i mentalnych ćwiczonek. Dużą wartością jest forma zeszytu ćwiczeń, dzięki czemu wiedza nie pozostaje abstrakcyjna, lecz staje się czymś, co można od razu odnieść do własnego życia i relacji – zarówno romantycznych, jak i rodzinnych czy przyjacielskich. No i robienie zadań oraz wypełnianie ankiet okazuje się bardzo pouczające. Można się zdziwić ;-) Oprócz opisu poszczególnych stylów przywiązania pojawia się tu przestrzeń na refleksję: nad przeszłością, utrwalonymi strategiami działania oraz nad tym, jak świadomie uczyć się wybierać inne, bardziej adekwatne reakcje. Książka pomaga zrozumieć, skąd biorą się nasze automatyczne zachowania w relacjach i jak stopniowo poszerzać repertuar swoich odpowiedzi. To proces oparty na analizie i powtarzalności – rozpoznanie schematu i wielokrotny, świadomy wybór innego działania pozwalają z czasem budować nowe, bardziej adekwatne odpowiedzi. Nie ma cudów, nasze style przywiązania są mocno utrwalone, ale można przestać je wzmacniać i zacząć poszerzać wachlarz swoich reakcji, zwłaszcza wtedy gdy te stare przestały być korzystne. Treść jest napisana bardzo klarownie, co sprawia, że książka jest dostępna także dla osób bez przygotowania psychologicznego. I wreszcie style przestają się mieszać. Mnie na przykład długo się mieszały styl unikający i lękowy. Przyczyny inne, ale byłam przeświadczona, że reakcje podobne. Dzięki przykładom zostało to bardzo obrazowo rozgraniczone i wyjaśnione. Książka łączy teorię z praktyką – wspiera w rozpoznawaniu własnego stylu przywiązania i jego skutków w kształtowaniu relacji, a zdobyta wiedza staje się pierwszym krokiem do korekty swoich zachowań by relacje międzyludzkie były bardziej sat

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: Jeśli szukacie kolejnego psychologicznego traktatu, który pozwoli Wam bezpiecznie schować się za murem teorii, Annie Chen ma dla Was złą wiadomość. Jej książka „Teoria przywiązania w praktyce” to nie wykład, a raczej kliniczny młotek, którym autorka systematycznie rozbija skorupę naszych relacyjnych nawyków. Publikacja wydawnictwa Laurum to hybryda poradnika i workbooka, która stawia sprawę jasno: samo czytanie o stylu lękowym czy unikającym niczego nie zmieni - trzeba zacząć działać! Prawdziwa praca zaczyna się tam, gdzie pojawia się ołówek i bolesna autorefleksja. Chen z chirurgiczną precyzją mapuje emocje, oferując „aktywne strategie leczenia” zamiast jałowych definicji. Największym atutem książki jest jej użyteczność i faktyczne znalezienie elementów, które nas w jakimś stopniu definiują. Rozróżnienie stylu lękowego od unikającego, które w teorii często się zlewa, tutaj zostaje rozdzielone za pomocą obrazowych scenariuszy i kwestionariuszy. Mimo, że całość bardzo mi “siadła” to muszę wetknąć szpilkę w starannie skrojoną strukturę pozycji. Chen wpada w pułapkę „tyranii wspomnień”. Większość ćwiczeń opiera się na formule „przypomnij sobie czas, kiedy...”. Dla osób z deficytami pamięci autobiograficznej lub tych, którzy mechanizmy obronne przekuli w amnezję dziecięcą, książka może stać się frustrującym murem nie do przebicia. Brakuje tu „akademickiego mięsa” czyli danych i badań, które uspokoiłyby bardziej sceptycznych, analitycznych czytelników. Niektóre zadania ocierają się o infantylność, co przy tak ciężkim temacie jak trauma więzi, może budzić opór. To pozycja dla tych, którzy nie boją się „pobrudzić sobie rąk” własną przeszłością. Jeśli jednak szukacie naukowego pogłębienia tematu, możecie odczuć delikatny niedosyt. To solidny, rzemieślniczy elementarz, taki doskonały na start, ale wymagający uzupełnienia o bardziej „mięsistą” literaturę naukową. Książkę do recenzji dostałem dzięki uprzejmości Wydawnictwa Laurum Ocena: 3,64/5 (goodreads 4/5 | lubimyczytać 7/1

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: Overall a pretty good workbook. A lot of recap about each attachment style from something like Attached but not as brief and concise as the 12 step workbook i read recently. Other thoughts/things I found interesting: -"marriage researcher John Gottman has determined that for every negative feeling or interaction couples have, it takes at least five positive ones to restored a balance for a happy, healthy relationship." -I like the burnout chart on page 30. I think it can be used for things beyond relationships, but I like the system. -I liked the map your emotions exercise on page 35 -I think to avoidance inventory on page 57 is something I would like to return to what I need to check in with myself -a new goal: secure attachment! "You think about the future in plan for it, but you don't stress too much about the nuts and bolts or dwell on the past when things get challenging." -I like the list on page 90 of secure relationship skills. I would like to return to this when goal setting. I want to get to a place where I tolerate feedback well and not try to change the subject or anything like that. -found it interesting and enlightening that "one trait of being insecurely attached is that it is difficult to make decisions and feel settled with them." -I do do fear the avoidant avoidant interaction style on pages 119 and 120 could be a possible future so need to work towards not letting that be. -I want to try the exercise on page 138 about eye contact.

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: A very good and insightful book, and as it states, it is very much a workbook haha Giving a good overview of attachment theory and styles, it gave me start to understanding myself and those I interact with, especially those that are close. The first few chapters are quite rough, focusing on introspection to our lives and calling us to question where our insecurities (should we have them) come from. Like other therapy books I've read, it gives many ways to explore ourselves and then to continue on past the book to keep introspecting and working on the problems we find through it. I find a lot of the exercises helpful, and especially the last few chapters I will keep around and come back to them as I continue my own journey. Reading is always good, in many ways, but this book specifically I like for all of its exercises. It takes a bit longer to get through, but the work and effort felt more tangible for me, as someone who hasn't development my own system of notes yet.

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: Багато практичних порад які можна застосовувати для покращення своїх стосунків з друзями та близькими людьми. В основному авторка описує приклади і засоби з романтичних стосунків, але багато чого можна перенести і на дружні відносини. Це саме воркбук, тому багато завдань де треба згадувати свої моменти з життя і думати над тим що призвело до таких вчинків і які наслідки вони дали. Ця частина мені не дуже сподобалась, бо іноді дуже важко згадати щось конкретне про що питається в завданні. Часто я відчував ніби проводив терапію сам їз собою, дуже прикольно. Якщо у вас є бажання покращити своє життя в стосунках, ця книга однозначно для вас. Коротенька, практична і дієва. P.S.: Я просто випав з деяких прикладів в кінці книжки. Ну як можна якось відновлювати і продовжувати стосунки якщо тобі зрадили😭😭😭

book_title: Attachment Theory Workbook
review_body: Відео про типи привʼязаності почали мені попадатись в кінці серпня, і я в шоці, але тік ток щось знає, бо саме ця тема стала ключовою в подальші місяці. Я вірю, що все відбувається в потрібний час, і знання про типи привʼязаності визначили подальший мій напрям психологічної роботи, адже, як виявилось, тривожні люди схильні обирати собі в партнери уникаючих. It’s sad, but we have what we have. Я була в пошуку хороших книги на цю тему, і знайшла цей воркбук. Що тут скажеш, непогана книга для того, щоб ознайомитися з загальною інформацією на цю тему, як певний вступний екскурс. Є багато тестів та вправ, які допоможуть визначити власний тип привʼязаності і є вправи на покращення взаємодії між людьми, згідно їх типу. Не можу поставити 5, бо я очікувала глибшого аналізу та наукового підгрунття для пояснень, і більшість інформації я вже знала (thanks to Tik Tok) Загалом, якщо ви вже прочитали цю книгу і визначили свій тип привʼязаності, раджу подивитися відео в тік тоці на цю тему - styles/types of attachment, там ви знайдете ще більше інформації, навіть з прикладами з відомих фільмів та серіалів. Ще, також, цій книзі не було багатьох деталей та нюансів, адже виявляється є різні типи уникаючих, fearful avoidant та dismissive avoidant. Але що радує - можливо досягнути secure attachment. Якщо у вас тривожний чи уникаючий тип, то це не клеймо! Це лише означає те, що із-за «небезпечної» атмосфери в дитинстві сформувалися захисні механізми психіки, і зʼявився страх близькості, але це все можна виправити, якщо бути чесним з самим собою і віднайти відчуття безпеки всередині себе (медитації можуть в цьому допомогти. перевірено), і тоді приходить усвідомлення того, що не всі люди будуть нас ранити в близьких стосунках. Для кращого пізнання себе раджу почитати цю книгу

review_body: Gibson is a psychology educator with a Master’s in transpersonal psychology and two businesses where her role sounds most like a hybrid between guide and educator. Gibson is a bit agnostic, combining attachment theory with methods from mindfulness, cognitive behavioral therapy, hypnosis, and emotional focused therapy from Gary Craig, the RAIN method from Michele McDonald, and acceptance and commitment therapy. From these theories and techniques, Gibson has fashioned her own approaches for her own clients (again, not in the professional therapy sense) to transform their lives by understanding their attachment styles, being more mindful, and intentionally shifting how they related to others in their life. The book is easy to read and on the shorter side. It can be read within several hours. There are a few especially valuable things from this book besides its integrative approach to strategies for better mental health. The first in an attachment style quiz that presents different feelings, thoughts, and behaviors associated with the four different attachment styles. This not only familiarizes the reader with general profiles but allows for spotting attachment styles in themselves and others, maybe ever shifting ways of navigating attachment needs depending on the context. The second in the chapter on The Basic Four squared. These are short profiles of how each general attachment style might generally interact with the other attachment styles. This gives readers a very general overview of what people with various attachment styles might run into as far as fears and raw spots with one another. One unfortunate part of this section is the hypothetical people seem to be labeled the attachment styles. Gibson has only a helpful intent, but language matters and shapes our perceptions, and in no circumstance should someone be labeled an attachment style as an inflexible, rigid label. People are people who handle their relationship to vulnerability and potential changes in inti

review_body: Interesting and informative introduction to attachment theory and how it can be used in conjunction with things like meditation and CBT, but feels like it is trying to include too much information in a small number of pages. Certain parts could have been left out and others expanded upon (the relationship between different attachment styles for example). It also makes a point to stress that these styles are fluid and vary over time and different relationship types then promptly goes on to give examples defined entirely by one attached style even going as far as to refer to individuals by their set form of attachment “the dismissive-avoidant”

book_title: Attachment Theory: A Guide to Strengthening Relationships
review_body: I am truly convinced this is THE best book about attachment styles available out there! Especially if you are interested in fearful-avoidant style, this is the one book that will not only mention 'oh yeah, that exists and is pretty messed up' but will go into details and base a lot of examples on it. It doesn't simplify other types either; Anxious isn't just a craving for attention victim and avoidants aren't cold and distant all the time. It explains how different types can be triggered and how they are likely to react. It spends a lot of time explaining dynamic between various combinations- potential threads and benefits too (and yeah, they are NOT as basic as 'any type will be successful dating a secure type' or 'avoidants and anxious will never under any circumstance be happy with each other'- in fact it gives insight to surprising but logical findings in each scenario). It doesn't limit to romantic relationships only- it gives amazing examples of co-workers, friends and flatmates and how their conflicts arise due to their attachment styles and how both are likely to deal with it. It proves we are all on spectrum- something very simple but comforting to know as those who have been struggling with their attachment style might find out they are very secure in other areas of life and never actually thought of it before. Lastly, it offers a solution for each type (including secure) to better communication and enhance mutual understanding. It is a fantastic book for anyone interested in the topic. Whether you are confused how to manage your own triggers or you are struggling to understand behaviour of your friend/colleague/romantic partner/family member this is a great book to dive into and get that beautiful knowledge guide you.

In the manner of the women’s beauty magazines or Facebook quizzes, you can take a test and identify the attachment style you most readily adopt, read about typical attachment style couple pairings, and read about a few treatment methods that can encourage change. I had a hard time finishing this book because I was bored. Will be looking for a heartier book on this topic.

book_title: Attachment Theory: A Guide to Strengthening Relationships
review_body: A clear and precise introduction to four attachment styles: secure, anxious-preoccupied, dismissive-avoidant, and fearful-avoidant. Growing up, every one of us forms a unique attachment style (ways we bond with other people). A secure style is healthy, others—not so. According to the theory and specialists who practice it, we all have one dominant style of the four mentioned above. We can’t really choose it—it depends on the upbringing we had and how well our parents responded to our needs. For example, a person clingy and needy may have had a parent who wasn’t available for them because of how busy they were. Their absence may have caused them distress, thus any conflict provokes their inner fear of being left. Someone who seems cold, distant, and overly independent may have had neglectful caregivers who have hardly ever helped them. Such people can have a deep conviction that people are inherently unreliable and they can only trust themselves for their own survival. Those who seem to give mixed signals of love and withdrawal, may have had an unpredictable parental figure. Such parents may have been loving and comforting one day, but scary and brutal another. Love, for them, is never stable. And, finally, those who trust easily and communicate freely most likely had caregivers who fulfilled their needs for stability, so they needn’t worry about their ability to form a bond. Overall, really insightful. After you learn to identify your own attachment style, the author gives you numerous ways to work on it. Every one of us can develop a secure attachment with some effort—none of it is made in stone. Sadly, I expected more depth in the theoretical part, so it is a book only for total beginners.

This book was highly informative, enlightening, validating, and eye-opening. Reading 'Attachment Theory' has made me more aware of my attachment style in different relationships (romantic, friendship, familial, job, etc) and has inspired me to dig deeper to better understand any of the 'insecure' attachment behaviors and thinking I may naturally exhibit that I can work on. This is truly an excellent book to begin to study attachment theory and to understand how and why you are the way you are in your relationships with others. From secure attachment styles to insecure attachment styles Gibson goes into great detail and example scenarios of different pairings of attachment styles in a multitude of scenarios to better explain the concepts. Gibson also explains the courses of action that can be taken with each insecure attachment style to begin the process of healing and relational improvement reassuring that there is hope beyond trauma and deeply-ingrained beliefs. I love this book! It truly taught me so much.

review_body: I was not a fan of this book. It has some good basic information about attachment styles, but it could have been communicated in about 20 pages. The rest of the book takes the form of advice on how to have fulfilling relationships, and it is saturated with the mononormative bias of the author. The traditional lifelong monogamous pair-bond, throughout the entire book, is held up as the shining pinnacle of relationships and is assumed to be everyone's goal. Any desire for autonomy is evidence of an avoidant attachment style and should be resisted. Ditto for any outside sexual interest (which is experienced by almost everyone). Codependence is encouraged as the mark of a secure attachment. There is also a clear favoritism toward a secure attachment style, which is to be expected as it is generally viewed as the healthiest style (and evidence supports this view). But there is also a favoritism toward anxious attachment style over avoidant. Partners of people with anxious attachment style are encouraged just to accommodate their partner's clinginess, constant need for reassurance, possessiveness, and jealousy, while partners of people with avoidant attachment style are encouraged to leave the relationship or else accept that they will never be completely happy. There is very little advice given on how to make an avoidant partner feel safe experiencing intimacy. Most advice regarding avoidant style is on how to change it. I was also unhappy with the presentation of each attachment style being unique to a person instead of unique to a relationship. That is not my experience of attachment styles. With some partners, I have a secure attachment style. With others, I can be anxious or avoidant. It's not because any one of these is my innate attachment style. It is because I am reacting to my partner's feelings and behavior. I have noticed this with other people also. My experience is that people do not have a discrete attachment style that gets implemented with every partner.

The worst thing you can do is to put on one of their labels, and use that as an excuse not to take a deeper look at your actions. This is a harmful book that will mislead you on your quest for a healthy, loving relationship.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: The first (and maybe only) thing to understand about attachment theory, is that attachment is simply a fancy word for love. Plain and simple. Once you understand that, the rest of the theory makes perfect sense. The next thing to know is that our patterns of bonding and repairing are conditioned i.e. learned, beginning in relationship between caregivers and infants, and continuing into adulthood. The last thing to know is that our relational conditioning i.e. attachment style can be problematic, but it can also change for the better over time, particularly with intentional therapeutic work. And understanding attachment theory can be an instrumental part of that process of therapeutic change. So what exactly is attachment theory? I'm glad you asked. Attachment theory began in the 1940's as a way to describe patterns of infant and caregiver bonding. It is one of the first psychological theories to integrate evolutionary theory. As such, it represented a radical departure from the dominant psychological theories of the time e.g. Freudian and Behaviorist orientations. Attachment Theory survived (in part) due to its simplicity and profound explanatory power. The creators of attachment theory (John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth) posited that mammals (particularly humans) evolved the capacity to deeply, emotionally connect with their young due to the relatively long period of infant dependence, circa 50 years (and counting) if one were to use my case as an example. Attachment theory asserted that if mammals (particularly humans) and their young fail to bond (i.e. attach), than the young are very likely to not survive, and the parents would then have failed to pass on their genes. review_body: Don’t be fooled by the title. The title is like wishy washing voodoo magic to suddenly make a sparkly relationship appear. And that’s bullshit of course. The actual content of the book is not bullshit though. It opened my eyes, and so many puzzle pieces finally came together. The premise is that your childhood, but also any experience you had afterwards with intimate relationships, lead to certain attachment patterns. If you’re lucky, you’re securely attached. If you’re slightly less lucky, you might be avoidant or anxious. What I also like about it is that it is acknowledging these attachment patterns without saying that there’s something wrong with you. They come from the cards we got dealt in life, and these patterns also make us who we are. Yes, getting yourself to a more secure stage will help, but until you get there, accept who you are, and try to slowly get yourself on the right path.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: An interesting read that will leave you thinking about all of the relationships in your life! It was heavily focused on romantic relationships but I do think a lot of the same information could be applied to other relationships in your life- friend, parents, co-workers. While we may be overall secure in one relationship we could be anxious in another and avoidant in another. Food for thought. Would recommend.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book is really good at telling you the different types of attachments people have in relationships and how to actively go about relationships in a secure way. We are all different in relationships but I think this book is a good tool in communicating effectively to make sure you and your partner understand each other and can have a healthy happy relationship.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I thought I was careful enough, insightful enough to not need self-help books on love and relationships to navigate how to be with someone, and who to be with. But after having recently found myself out of a painful relationship, I've come to realize how far off base I was. It scared the guts out of me to see how easily I had chained myself in a relationship that had made me incredibly miserable, and from which I hadn't been able to leave until the other one left. I found this book when seeking out some kind of answer, an explanation to what went wrong and why: why it was so bad, and I still stuck around. And, I have to say, this book delivered. The idea that we can all be summarized into three main attachment styles stems from developmental psychology and it's well-studied. I'm not sure about how well recognized it is when applied to adult love relationships. I found them pretty unstable and flickery, better ascribable for roles in specific relationships than for fixed personality traits (e.g., from memory, childhood attachment styles do not seem to transfer to adulthood, adult attachment styles change every 6-7 years) But, I've found myself, and some of my ex partners and past relationships reflected in many of the scenarios described in the book as highly unstable, based on two people with opposing anxious and avoidant styles. It was enlightening and legitimizing to hear hurtful memories recognized as signs that something is wrong, if a bit painful. I already knew about the neurobiological basis of attachment, but I've found it particularly helpful to hear it applied in order to justify why we might stick to relationships that hurt us. It was comforting to know that the pain of leaving a relationship, even a bad one, stems from our biological need to find a secure attachment, and that sometimes that need ends up getting associated with the wrong stimulus: someone that is not going to deliver back in that attachment. Thus, it's important to be careful about activa

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I’ve spent 32 years asking myself, “Why can’t I be like the cool girls and be in a stable relationship? I’m so dramatic and I end up alone!” And here, this entire time, it’s simply been that I have an anxious attachment style. And society “says” that being mysterious, distant, and chill is the only acceptable way to be in a relationship. Well, I’m not mysterious - I wear my heart on my sleeve; I’m not distant - I want physical and emotional connection; and I’m not chill - I’m expressive, have needs, and want attention. And there is nothing wrong with that! If someone can’t or doesn’t want to give me that, then they aren’t the right fit for me. And I’m not for them! It is incredibly liberating to accept yourself for who you are, understand why you act certain ways, and to articulate specifically what you need to do to achieve the goal you want: a kind, loving, supportive, and long-lasting relationship. I highly recommend this book for anyone struggling to effectively communicate in a romantic relationship or who always seems to “date the wrong kind of person.” There may be a specific reason for that and this book can help explain it and address it. I will continue to refer to it in the future! Favorite Quotes: 1. Attachment principles teach us that most people are only as needy as their unmet needs. review_body: this was excellent and very needed at this point in my life. it felt like it was written specifically with me in mind - I vividly remember having the exact thoughts/feelings as some examples listed out in this book but thinking, ironically, that there’s no way this is ‘normal’. key take away is that while many people could make things work, it shouldn’t have to be painful and compromising all the time. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: 4,0 estrelas. Este livro, que li duas vezes e que terei de ir relendo até embeber os ensinamentos, princípios e estratégias apresentados, veio numa altura de convulsão. Depois de ler em alguns canais de YouTube sobre a teoria da vinculação afectiva em adultos e fazer um assessment on-line para perceber (confirmar) qual o meu estilo de vinculação, achei importante a leitura deste livro que é até referido em muitos desses canais. É o que é, o meu estilo de vinculação é o desorganizado. Para quem não está familiarizado com a teoria e modelo desenvolvidos por John Bowlby, o modelo identifica 3 estilos principais no modo como os seres humanos se vinculam aos outros, sobretudo quem lhes está mais próximo. O estilo seguro, que é referido no livro cerca de 50% das pessoas tem (numa nota paralela devo referir que acho essa % alta mas posso ser eu). 30% das pessoas tem um estilo ansioso. 20% tem um estilo evitante. Grosso modo e em grandes números é essa a distribuição. Repararão que o somatório ascende a cerca de 90%. Isto porque uma minoria das pessoas, pensa-se que 10% ou menos, tem um estilo que mistura as características da vinculação ansiosa com a vinculação evitante. Esse estilo é conhecido como ansioso-evitante ou desorganizado. Do que me conheço, e os assessment que fiz parecem confirmar, é esse o meu estilo de vinculação. É sem dúvida um estilo altamente desafiador na relação com os outros pois mistura o pior (e o melhor vá) de cada um dos estilos ansioso e evitante. Uma pena o livro não se debruçar mais sobre este estilo muito particular e desenvolver ao longo das suas 300 páginas muito mais os estilos ansioso, evitante e seguro. Nalgumas críticas a esta obra li que leitores, normalmente evitantes, reclamam do viés dos autores sobre esse estilo que parece um pouco estigmatizado. Quase numa óptica de mau da fita causadores do sofrimento de todo o mundo e demais estilos, sobretudo o ansioso. Não vou tão longe mas percebo a frustração de quem, como eu, tem traços de e

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: An interesting insight into attachment theory and romantic relationships. This book prompted me to reflect on relationships I have experienced in my life. The learnings from this book were highly applicable and will likely help me be a better partner in future.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Thoroughly enjoyed this as a great intro to attachment styles & how to recognize healthy/unhealthy behaviors and responding to them. Highly recommend! There's lots of examples/stories so it's an easy read.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This was okay. I was hoping for something a little meatier, but my understanding is that this is more or less the intro book and that true armchair psychologists will move on to other books. Some observations/mild complaints: 1) I was really hoping for them to address anxious/avoidant types, after throwing it out there briefly that such unicorns exist. 2) I was slightly frustrated by the neat sorting into the three types (see above). While I've always known I was anxious about my relationships (even if I didn't have the jargon to label it with), it seems like my experience shows more of a continuum. I guess that's not such a departure from their ideas, but the portrayal seemed a little overconfident and/or oversimplified. 3) Admission: I didn't actually do the exercises. It's highly probable that I would find them effective. The thing that most tripped me up (other than a counterproductive but deeply ingrained distaste for "workbooks") was the idea of finding a "secure model" to emulate. I guess some people immediately think of someone they know who models ideal security in relationships, but no one sprang to mind, and the idea of imagining an ideal version of myself (which was another option they gave), while appealing, was more effort than I wanted to make while reading it. 4) I was struck by the fact that almost all of the examples were heterosexual couples. It just seemed a little odd, and gave sort of a late-20th-century Mars-and-Venus vibe. Or maybe I've just read too many of that kind of book. However, if I had been reading it as anything other than a heterosexual in a heterosexual relationship, it probably would have been bothersome. I wouldn't *not* recommend this, but I hope my next foray into the subject will be a little more nuanced and detailed. I do think that this would be good reading for someone who isn't obsessed with dissecting their inner workings but who has a vague sense of dissatisfaction with how they function in relationships. It would proba

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: My best friend always jokes with me "you can't change the people around you but you can change the people around you". As ironic as it seems, this makes sense to me - a person with an anxious attachment style. I'm sure there are people who are dissatisfied with how the author spent way too much volume discussing the anxious-avoidant dynamic while leaving out the rest. Especially the secure attachment styled readers won't benefit much from reading this book. However, I like that the author goes deep into the evolutionary ties of attachment theory from prehistoric times (how humans are heterogeneous species and we vary greatly). Attachment theory is based on the assertion that the need to be in a close relationship is embedded in our genes. Throughout evolution, genetic selection favored people who became attached because it provided a survival advantage. So it's partially true that your childhood is not all why you are so clingy/ avoidant. Some people are just born that way, and changing something as deep as their gene is a lot of work. I'm not saying let's just leave our partners whenever difficulties occur, but there are toxic relationships that are not meant to be fixed. If you're unhappy after having tried every way to make things work, chances are that you should move on. It's in your best interest to end a dysfunctional relationship rather than get stuck forever with the wrong person just because they make you feel loved once a month/ suffocated with constant guilt trips and missed calls. Our culture encourages people with anxious attachment styles to believe that many of their needs are illegitimate (thus we have the "cool girl" trope, ughh). But whether they are legitimate or not for someone else is beside the point. On the other hand, people with avoidant attachment styles are shamed for their cold hearts. In reality, avoidant people often perceived as the mood setter, the cooler person in a relationship, but are they, really? I have been both anxious and av

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I cannot recommend this book to anyone who has a tendency toward being avoidant. The author has a tendency to glorify secure people, coddle anxious people, and vilify avoidant people. The latter are supposedly cold, manipulative, and jealous. Anxious people should find a secure partner. Avoidant people should change. And on premise, I don't disagree. Most picked up this book for self-realisation and -improvement. As someone on the avoidant side, I expected to read about how to avoid less. But what I got was a list of things such as "don't glorify your ex partner" or "let go off the idea of the one" (those are the most harmless ones). But that is very unhelpful if that's not the reason why one is avoidant. Avoidant people just are ... avoidant (I have a feeling this will come as a surprise to the author). The author consistently links avoidant with being active (through manipulation, vocally dismissing partners, or making partners jealous??) when avoidant in itself is just through its definition passivity; you avoid doing anything. As someone who mostly seems to fall into the avoidant category, I would much rather disengage from situations and/or let relationships quietly fade away rather than addressing my struggles, because that's *hard*. But the author seems to insist that avoidant people need to stop *checks list* playing games and making their partners jealousy. He insists that somehow, people who avoid (in itself, again, a passive activity), need to stop being so active about their hatred for their partners. But that's not really the truth. My past partners were all decent people (not perfect pour moi, but, you know, not creepy). The relationships failed because I was incapable of communicating and instead, yes, you guessed it, avoid talking about grand concepts like feelings. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: EPIPHANY VENT: On my little journey to understand my relationship with love and intimacy, I think this book has been one of the most eye opening and important ones I’ve read on the subject. It’s made me reflect a lot on my past relationships and those I’ve been surrounded by, and it’s helped me recognise how I have an avoidant attachment style as it acted as my safety blanket growing up. I’ve always been very scared of intimacy and security, only seeing it break down around me and cause pain in my childhood. I’ve never allowed myself to rely on someone else, to be emotional and vulnerable with someone because the two people who raised me and meant to provide that, never did. This meant when someone came to offer me a secure base, it was a new language to me and it was terrifying. I saw relying on someone as a weakness, I was scared they’d manipulate me, use me. The only security I ever truly experienced growing up was within myself, which is crazy thinking when I’ve battled with depression and anxiety - how was that a safe space? I feared it would take away my independence if I offered my heart and life to someone, as all I had known my whole life is to be me myself and I. This mind set was then reinforced by societies obsession with the romanticised concept of the ‘independent woman’ who thrives of being alone. Yes we don’t need a partner and we do need to break those patriarchal assumptions, but the fact is it’s quite darn lovely having one and we need to stop seeing it as a weakness. I grew up in a space that didn’t invite effective communication or emotional conversations. I never saw what a secure base looks like or a healthy or happy relationship in fact, I put up barriers as defence mechanism, thinking only I can save myself and look after me, and it’s heart breaking realising yes it may have protected and saved my in my childhood, but it’s sabotaging my adult life and happiness now. So this book has enlightened me and held me accountable to change my mindset

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: full review for Sasha! I expected this book to explore more psychology but in reality it was a self-help book that referenced pretty tenuous evidence without explaining the /why/ (e.g. the word association experiment that they kept pulling HUGE generalizations from which simply did not seem justified and required further evidence or explanation). Plus it seemed to be a self-help book that would only help anxiously attached people -- many of the other reviews point out how the author treats anxious attachment as their special misunderstood children and avoidants as the emotionally dead partners from hell. I will say that as a mostly secure/occasionally anxious person I did feel validated in some parts, but the validation so heavy-handed and patronizing that I more often responded with eye-rolling. Regarding securely attached people, the book says that most of the population is securely attached and they are all confident and fabulous communicators, which from anecdotal experience seems like a stretch. Much of the thesis is about creating healthy communication and asking for what you need, which is great and universal advice! However, the overreliance on attachment theory went in some weird directions and created excuses for unhealthy relationship tendencies. For example, one of the earlier chapters talks about "the myth of codependency" and is basically like don't be ashamed of codependency, you just have so much love to give!! Despite mostly addressing anxious people the book maybe never talks about setting healthy boundaries, at least not in depth, and gives many examples where the anxious person has porous/toxic boundaries and the author just suggests making that your partner's problem because hey, that's just your style! book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: In "Attached: The New Science of Adult Attachment and How It Can Help You Find and Keep Love," Amir Levine introduces us to the world of adult attachment, which is divided into three main styles: Anxious, Avoidant, and Secure. The examples given in the book are so relatable and insightful that I could not only easily place the people I know into these categories, but I also started seeing these patterns in fictional characters. This goes to show how universal these concepts are, making the book not just an exploration of others' behaviors but also a mirror reflecting our own attachment styles. The book encourages taking a quiz on their website to find out your attachment style. However, the depth and clarity of the examples in the book made it somewhat straightforward for me to identify with one of the styles, almost making the quiz an additional rather than essential tool for understanding. Early on, the authors emphasize the importance of recognizing these attachment styles, even suggesting that incompatible pairings should consider ending things in the early stages. This felt a bit extreme to me, casting a shadow of doubt over the initial chapters. However, as I progressed through the book, I was pleased to find a shift towards the importance of communication. This later focus offers a beacon of hope for navigating differences, proving to be a more balanced approach than the initial impression might suggest. While the book does an excellent job of exploring these three attachment styles, it's important to note that my awareness of other types, such as 'fearful' or 'disorganized,' comes from external sources, as the book does not delve into these. This isn't necessarily a flaw but something to keep in mind for readers seeking a comprehensive understanding of all possible attachment styles. Overall, "Attached" is a fascinating read that provides practical advice and real-life examples that resonate deeply with personal and observed experiences. It's a book that not

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Well, this was a weird read. I picked this book up to complement by studies, and because I'm interested in the psychology of relationships and attachment. Which might explain why I found this book really strange. It provides a basic primer for (some) adult attachment styles, and there are elements which I found interesting, and even helpful. But overall, it was way too simplified, and almost lacked nuance and depth when discussing the complexities of adult relationships. One of the biggest things I couldn't wrap my head around, was the insistence from the authors that dysfunctional attachment styles can be simply healed by finding a secure partner. The biggest example of this was the Marsha and Craig case study. The authors spend almost 5 pages dedicated to Marsha's (anxiously-attached) relationship. She describes years of borderline emotional and verbal abuse from her partner, and when we get to the end of the story, she finally leaves him and all is well because she found a secure partner who doesn't treat her like rubbish. That's where it ends. All is well with Marsha because now she's with a secure partner? Is there no room for an anxiously-attached partner to heal WITHOUT getting into a relationship?! This seems to be the central message of the book - it is the responsibility of your partner to fix you. To attend to you. To make sure your attachment-systems aren't triggered. Which is just something I fundamentally disagree with. Not to mention the risk of enmeshment that can happen in long-term relationships where the lines of responsibility are blurred - which ultimately leads to dissatisfaction. But the authors also seem to think that intimacy breeds more closeness and better sex, which is also categorically incorrect. Other reviewers have mentioned the weird bias the authors have against the avoidantly-attached, so I won't go into that too much. One of the best psychology books available to the general public; many are just dumbed down or opinion based. This is not one of those. I reiterate, this is a great starting point to understand attachment styles and how they develop/affect our adult relationships. 10/10

review_body: I give this book 1 star, here's why, their study is flawed-50% of the population is SECURE- on what planet are the authors living on? They even say on page 140, that the study is inconclusive on adults. That would make sense, cause as each age is reached, and if the need for that age is not met, insecurity increases. Then the authors debunk, the codependent/dependent relationship, that says, "needing" someone is not healthy. Needing someone for your security needs is not healthy, and is practiced everyday as the codependent/dependent relationship. But the authors embrace, Depending on each other. Depending on each other is very healthy, but is not practiced in everyday life, as one person is either the caretaker or dependent. The knowledge of attachment is not new and there is a much better book out there called, The Two Step by Eileen McCann, focusing on the ANXIOUS (SEEKER) AND AVOIDANT (SOUGHT) in a simple but profound detail. I don't mean to be disrespectful, but the authors come from privileged backgrounds. Their attachment needs have been met at a much higher rate, than the average person. So, maybe in their circle 50 % of the population is secure? The Anxious (seeker) and Avoidant (sought) is very prevalent in our society. Their fears of abandonment and engulfment, and their opposing behavior of Power and Distance are challenging to overcome. CAN YOU OVERCOME YOUR ATTACHMENT STYLE TO CREATE, A SECURE FOUNDATION WITHIN, FOR TRUE INTIMACY? BUT, THEN AGAIN THE AUTHORS OF THIS BOOK, FEEL AS LONG AS YOU FIND THE RIGHT PERSON, WHO WILL NOT TRIGGER YOUR ATTACHMENT ISSUES, YOU WILL EXPERIENCE PEACE AND HAPPINESS TOGETHER FOREVER- GOOD LUCK!

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: My therapist recommended me this. It was fine. Mostly did not apply to me because I am not in a relationship nor am I particularly looking for one. Also we’ve determined that my attachment style is disorganized and this book mentions it like once just to say it’s rare and then never addresses it again…super helpful. I got the feeling that people with secure attachment styles were put on a pedestal. The book implies that people with secure attachment styles are all amazing communicators who know exactly how to react in each and every conflict, and I doubt that’s the best generalization to make. I appreciated the examples of effective communication though.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: A thought-provoking introduction into adult attachment theory with clearly a lot of research and anecdotes to back up the discussion. It’s an easy read with helpful workbook-like exercises to substantively engage the reader and allow them to sift through the nuances of what’s being claimed. Though I did appreciate the read, I take issue with some of the claims being made and wish there was greater detail into how one’s attachment preferences are derived. The way the book is written appears to paint a hierarchal class structure with the “precious secures” (their words, not mine) reigning supreme, followed by the “anxious”, and then very distantly followed by the “avoidants”. There was one “CYA” chapter on Effective Communication which I appreciated, but the vast majority of the book very strongly sought out to validate the needs of an anxious type but didn’t explore validation/justification for avoidants which feels especially harmful since the book claims that our attachment types tend to stay consistent. Perhaps because of the lack of a sufficient “origin story” for one’s attachment type, I had a hard time justifying the presented figures (50% of the population are secure, 25% anxious, 25% avoidant). I also didn’t understand why attachment types couldn’t be more fluid. I’m weary of anything that tries to make sweeping judgment and while I appreciated the read and believe there is some insight to be taken, I’m still left underwhelmed and frustrated.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: 3.5/5.0 比起討論依附關係為何因人而異，這本書的重點是實用性，從理解自己的依附風格、分析伴侶的依附風格、到給不同組合的建議，這本書最值得一看的就是「如何應對」 也許依附理論不是非黑即白，有些測驗甚至有第四種混合型風格，但在書裡的各種案例與分析中，讀者也能多少看到自己與伴侶的行為特徵，比起其他談論依附關係的書，我覺得這本很適合入門的讀者

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Amir Levine e Rachel Heller explicam a teoria da vinculação e o seu impacto nas relações de uma forma extremamente simples e fácil de compreender. Sucintamente, a teoria da vinculação baseia-se na premissa de que a relação que estabelecemos com os nossos cuidadores durante a infância influencia diretamente a maneira como nos relacionamos na vida adulta. Mais ainda, a teoria revela que quando dependemos seguramente de alguém, isto é, nos sentimos confortáveis para procurar o seu conforto e apoio (quer seja um cuidador, na infância, ou um parceiro, na vida adulta), temos mais facilidade para explorar aquilo e aqueles que nos rodeiam. Assim, paradoxalmente, para sermos pessoas mais independentes e seguras de si mesmas, necessitamos de depender de terceiros. Embora seja, por vezes, uma perspetiva redutora da teoria da vinculação, o livro apresenta ideias essenciais para o bom funcionamento das relações na vida adulta, assim como estratégias úteis e práticas (e.g. comunicação efetiva) para estabelecer relações mais saudáveis e gratificantes. Conhecimento é poder, e compreendermos a forma como nós e quem nos rodeia está "programado" para funcionar em situações de intimidade, assim como podemos tornar essa programação mais funcional, é essencial. Desta forma, Attached é uma leitura importante para qualquer pessoa que esteja ou procure estar numa relação.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Attached classifies people as having one of three attachment styles: Secure, Avoidant, and Anxious I feel that this book could help people with what they classify as an "anxious attachment style" the most, followed closely by "avoidant". According to the book, my husband and I both have "secure attachment styles", and this I don't feel that it benefited me very much. I didn't read it in hopes that it would turn around a failing marriage, or turn on some lightbulb as to why we argue, because that isn't the case at all. I am actually quite happy in my marriage, but I enjoy informing myself on communication styles and how to better myself not only in my romantic relationship, but in platonic ones as well. The only reason that I've given this book 3 stars, is because I did not really learn much from it to help myself. As I said, I feel that someone with an anxious attachment style could greatly benefit from the book if they took the information to heart. Another thing I really liked about the book, is that it did not focus on religion. I am not a religious person and have always had a difficult time finding a book that did not relate romantic back to God and religion.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: pretty standard in its heteronormativity :/ but super enlightening in how the 3 main types - anxious, avoidant, secure (based on coping mechanisms, trauma responses, etc) - can set up a (romantic) relationship for failure, heartbreak, and influences our continuously re-traumatizing patterns from which we interact with others. it has a lot of stories, which definitely helps de-personalize hurtful interactions, allowed me to move out of some stuck places after a really hard break-up, and it offers some great ideas about how to communicate to de-escalate situations/patterns both short-term and long-term, by getting to the heart of what is coming up for someone as they're getting activated. it also helps you become more aware of how to stop falling into the same patterns and cycles of hurt by being more attuned to the information someone is offering you in your first interactions, and how that escalates when we ignore those red flags and signals. i've been using this lens for all my relationships as well as watching how people interact/what's coming up for when people aren't feeling heard, as someone who does a lot of conflict mediation/resolution work and its been DEEPLY useful!

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I highly recommend "Attached" for anyone interested in learning about attachment and how it influences relationships. I promise -- your attachment style and how it meshes with your partner's influences how satisfied you are with your relationship. Understanding that impact can be all the difference in whether the relationship thrives, fizzles out, or blows up. A caution: The beginning of the book implies that certain relationships just aren't going to work out -- not great news if you're already married or otherwise deeply committed to someone whose attachment style clashes with yours. Hang in there, though. Levine does a wonderful job describing attachment styles and helping readers determine where they land. Quizzes are included for diagnosis of self and partner. Most importantly, Levine provides this wisdom: Your attachment style doesn't need to change. Energy spent on that goal is wasted. Instead, know yourself, know your needs, and ask for them in ways that increase the chances they'll be met.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: There are only about 15 reasonable pages in this book. And here's a concise summary: - If you have an anxious attachment style, everything is fine with you. Your emotional needs may be a bit more demanding, but if you date a secure person and work on communication skills, it should be fine. - If you have an avoidant attachment style, you are the problem. You're abusive, with everything being wrong with you. Your emotional needs are too low, and you have to change. - People with a secure attachment style are god blessed. Hopefully, they won't date avoidants. Although the authors may not intend it exactly as I described, while reading this, you consistently get these feelings. Furthermore, some examples of people with an avoidant attachment style are actually examples of abusers, rather than avoidants. And I think it’s really wrong to mix these two. Meanwhile, severe emotional manipulations by individuals with an anxious attachment style are often downplayed, with the focus being on their emotional needs. written by a person with an anxious attachment style.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Wanted to give it 3 stars due to no mention of disorganised attachment style. Why did I give it 4 stars? • I liked how interactive it is. I liked the explanation with examples of which— some of them resonate with everyone who reads. • They mentioned important stuff in bullet points which makes it easier for us to read or to bookmark/remember it. • The exercises really helped me understand better and evaluate my own shit. This interactiveness also makes it less boring. Why not 5? Well, it didn't mention the disorganised style. Overall, it's a helpful book and I don't regret picking it up. I'm grateful for it. Personally, I don't feel that it's biased like some comments say. Would I recommend it to anyone? Maybe. But before they read the book, I would suggest them to go through different sources and to see if they resonate with either of the basic three attachment styles. If they're someone disorganised, it might not be as useful as it is to me. I don't know much about the disorganised style. It's always good to have different sources than a single one too.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book has been unbelievably helpful for me and I am so glad I read it. A few years ago after going through a difficult breakup I came across the concept of attachment styles and I completely see myself in this book as someone who was partnered with an avoidantly attached person and became more and more anxious as a result. It was so helpful for me to understand how these styles form, what kind of behaviour it results in, and what to look for in a future partner based on this. I cannot recommend this book enough, especially if you are anxious or have dated/are dating someone more avoidant. I just couldn’t believe how similar my experiences were to the ones that were discussed in the book. I can see if you are in a secure partnership that this may not be as helpful since you may not relate to these examples, but you never know, it could be really revealing for past relationships or even future ones (including friendships) as well.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Well written, bad content. Categorizes all people into three different categories, two of which are good and healthy and natural (secure and anxious), one of which is unhealthy and abusive (avoidant). Simplistic, heteronormative, monogomy-obsessed, and judgemental. Disappointing, especially because the general categories are vaguely interesting. Might have been better applied to relationships, rather than people - we are more complex than one archetype. Reading Kristin Dombek's "The Selfishness of Others: An Essay on the Fear of Narcissism" is a good venue for understanding the urge to soothe anxious people by telling them that there's nothing wrong with them - there's something wrong with your partner. For those with anxious tendencies, the authors recommend finding someone secure who can fulfill your every need, quickly and effectively. For those with avoidant tendencies, the authors recommend not dating until you've overcome your own personality.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: 2.5 stars rounded down. Although there was some great info in here about anxious-avoidant traps, protest and deactivation behavior, and effective communication, I felt disappointed overall. I’m not someone who has an avoidant attachment style but this book really seems to villainize those who do and provides mostly information that caters to anxiously attached people. There are some scenarios where they even go so far as equating emotional abuse to having an avoidant attachment style. Additionally I feel that they ignored a lot of the psychological discomfort and anxiety that is involved in avoidant patterns. The book also doesn’t address disorganized attachment basically at all and doesn’t discuss how childhood trauma and attachment to parental figures, friendships and relationships in youth, and other factors shape how we attach to others. Not to mention the book focuses entirely and solely on cis-het relationships.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Somewhat underwhelming. The key messages: - Your emotional needs are valid and must be met. - Anxious + Avoidant relationships do not work, so save yourself some heartache and choose a Secure partner. - Open and honest communication is essential. That's it. I'm convinced the Attachment theory has some merit when applied to romantic relationships. However, I feel it's not so black-and-white and you can't really squeeze most persons into one of the three boxes (Secure, Anxious, Avoidant). And if you can't do that, then the rest of the book quickly becomes either not relevant (as it's talking about strongly classified individuals), or to generic and common-sense (open communication is important, etc., etc.). My suggestion: read the first part about the research, but skip/skim the less interesting parts.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: The book covers the three attachment styles in relationships; avoidant, secure and anxious. It discusses how relationships work and what combinations might work better than others, in addition to what to do in case you are in a relationship with opposite styles (anxious and avoidant). According to the authors, you should avoid an anxious-avoidant relationship (almost at all costs) because it is kind of "unworkable" but, just in case you are in such relationship, then it offers also what could be done to minimize its negative impacts. The authors also state that while attachment style might be deeply rooted in us and shaped in early childhood, it does not mean it is set in stone for life and moving in and out from anxious or avoidant to a more secure position is possible. Things that help in doing so is also discussed in later chapters.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I learned about attachment theory in a psych class back in college. I happened to take the class right after the end of a long term anxious-avoidant relationship that triggered my attachment system so frequently that I hardly recognized myself by the end of it. Learning about attachment styles was so incredibly eye opening, validating, and above all healing. I have this fantasy that someday styles will be asked/discussed during dating as openly and with as little judgement as a person's zodiac sign in the US or asking blood type in Japan, for example. This book is an excellent tool towards understanding, mending, and heading towards a happy healthy relationship for a person of any relationship status or attachment type.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Exactly what I needed to learn right now. The information I found in here was life-changing, and I do not exaggerate. But the overall principles in the science of adult attachment were still the same and will make a huge difference in how I view and handle my current and future relationships, and even more my eventual main relationship. (You know it had to be good if I read a NONFICTION book in ONE week while I was in the middle of 5 other fiction books.) I recommend to every one of my adult friends. I think there is something each can take from it.

review_body: Overall, I found the main argument compelling: that as humans we crave emotional intimacy and there are four main categories of behavior that summarize how humans respond to this need. The book is easy to read and has some useful exercises for analyzing ways to better communicate your intimacy needs with a partner. However, I do have a couple of frustrations with this book. Aside from one brief mention in the introduction, they completely fail to consider the fourth category, anxious-avoidant (also known as fearful-avoidant), for the reason that anxious-avoidant types make up only a "meager" 4% of the population. However, I found this choice of omission frustrating for a couple of reasons. First, 4% is a sizeable amount of any population and at least merits a paragraph explaining how this category differs from the other three. Second, it left me feeling like a quarter of the theory was missing. I wanted to understand how attachment theory works as a whole, and unfortunately, this was the not the comprehensive book on this psychological theory. However, I felt like the book generalized behavioral patterns far too much. (Then again, what did I expect? It is a "pop psych" book.) For example, they do not discuss the possibility that some people might exhibit a combination of behaviors from more than one of the three main categories. It assumes that because most people show a preference for one category of behavior over the others, this person is therefore, definitively, either anxious or avoidant or secure, in all romantic relationships. And if a typically anxious or typically avoidant person doesn't exhibit behaviors typical of their attachment type, fret not for it's simply lying dormant and will rear its ugly head again when triggered by the wrong partner. review_body: I learned a lot from reading this book about the three- four, I guess, counting anxious-avoidant- attachment styles, and how they all interact with each other. Particularly, I was struck by the dependency paradox. Our generation has convinced itself that people don’t need each other- that, as a matter of fact, we are at our best when we are independently happy, living in a state of self-reliance with no complaints. That sentiment continues even as it pertains to relationships: the sentiment I see on social media all the time is that a relationship should be two completely wholly individual people functioning on their own and sharing their separate worlds, which theoretically is great. But biologically speaking, having a partner is an evolutionary survival tactic. Humans are not an independent species. And when we have a partner, our bodies and our literal biologies sync together, almost to make one physical unit. We are responsible for each other’s well-beings, not only emotionally then, but physically. We come to depend on each other for wellness in a partnership by design. But the paradoxical thing is that biological dependency generates the ability for authentic independence: if we have a rock or anchor, this makes it safe for us to enter the world on our own and know someone has our backs. These are simple ideas, but it blew my mind because I truly had internalized the idea of necessary isolation in a relationship. I like that they end the book on the note that love should not be left up to chance. That a relationship can be saved by effective communication skills, compromise, and some oxytocin. It took the mystery out of why certain people work together and others don’t. It makes a model out of people with secure attachment and hits on the importance of having secure models to teach insecure people how to function in a healthy way in relationships. The chapter of advice for avoidantly attached people was short and had far less reframes and tools than that for other attachment styles. Many stories ended in an avoidantly attached person alone and lonely, with some implicit degree of smugness about the avoidants' pain. Danced around the claim that relationships with avoidant people are doomed, that all types are incompatible with avoidant people. Didn't talk about fearful avoidant style much if at all. A lot of the tools provided were great and immediately applicable tools, but I wish there were more discussion of healing from attachment wounds over the course of years (beyond simply emphasizing the importance of secure relationships) and earning a secure attachment style. It also left a lot of kinds of love out. It was amatonormative (putting romantic love on a pedestal above family love, community love, friendship love, spiritual love, etc.) - attachment science is relevant to relationships with friends and family as well as lovers and it barely touched on this. It also totally left out any discussion of non-monogamy, which is disappointing as the non-monogamy community has developed some deep insights about healthy relationships and attachments. I did appreciate that it featured many stories about queer relationships, although more explicit discussion of queerness and attachment (e.g. overview of any research findings, discussion of how hiding your sexuality, and internalized queerphobia can interplay with attachment, etc.) would have been great. Somme toute, j'ai principalement adoré la section sur la glorification des relations de type montagnes russes et le manque de distinction entre l'adrénaline conséquente aux blessures d'attachement réactivées et la « passion » des débuts de relation. De plus, je n'ai pas perçu que les évitant.e.s étaient dépeint.e.s comme des êtres insensibles, mais je peux certes comprendre le sentiment de certain.e.s. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: 4.75 stars? Apart from grabbing lunch in the middle, I read this in literally one sitting! I have a feeling that my reaction/review to this book may evolve over time, but my initial thoughts: In so many ways, this book made me feel seen. From the first paragraph, I quickly identified with the "anxious" attachment-type. This was helpful in that I was able to reimagine qualities that I have typically viewed as some of my fundamental personality flaws as not that uncommon, and also, helped remind me that people deal with relationships and intimacy in very different ways. For that perspective alone, I am grateful. Also, the Relationship Inventory was the closest thing to free therapy I've had in a while. By deliberately going through previous romantic experiences, even the ones seemingly trivially short, I was able to recognize previous interactions where I am less proud of my behavior, but also, was surprised to notice a distinct pattern of improvement from "anxious" to "secure" behaviors (though I certainly have a long way to go!) At the end of the day, one thing I had to continually remind myself of was that attachment theory does not explain everything with relationships (nor do the authors ever claim that it does). There are other factors -- like my extreme impatience, for example -- that come into play and warrant some other kinds of self-improvement. Relatedly, I had to often wrestle with the idea that even as an "anxious" type who can work towards adopting more "secure" behaviors, there are some people in the world who are simply not the right partner for me, and that is okay. Even as an "anxious" type, I am enough. In conclusion, an engrossing read that I will undoubtedly think back to many times. (The only reason for the 4.75 stars is that even after all that, there is a still a part of me that feels shitty for being "anxious" and wishes I were more naturally "secure," even though the authors do emphasize that attachment types are not fixed!)

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Interesting read and I got a lot out of this. I’d recommend this book to anyone interested in psychology, their attachment style in relationships or guidance on how to react/manage challenges in a relationship. Love the guided questions and real life examples, including the questionnaire and assessment link to determine your attachment style (secure with borderline avoidant attachment and I accept that proudly). Only reason I can’t rate this a 5 are due to the following experts that I just can’t wrap my head around or agree with. Getting comfortably close: the secure attachment style - in this chapter, an example of having a secure attachment style is Nathan who is in an awful marriage with someone who has extreme outbursts, has slapped him and is cheating on him. Nathan puts up with the abuse and disloyalty until his wife divorces him on her own terms. Yet this is a secure attachment style because he’s “forgiving” and “understands his partners needs and motives”. And “naturally secure people just naturally dwell less on the negative”. How the hell is that secure? To me, that’s anxious if you can’t walk away from a relationship like this nor realize your own self worth. The very end states “we alone are responsible for our emotional needs; they are not our partners responsibility” which I totally agree with. Yet the same paragraph opposedly then states “we must remind ourselves that in a true partnership both partners view it as their responsibilities to ensure the others emotional well-being”. If my secure/avoidant self could throw any quotes into this book it would be: “never put your happiness in someone’s hands. They’ll drop it every time.” And Will Smith’s “her happiness is not my responsibility. She should be happy and I should be happy individually. Then we come together and share our happiness. Giving someone a responsibility to make you happy when you can’t do it for yourself is selfish.” I remembered these quotes a lot during certain chapters (codependency

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Starting with the good: I like the framework of how the author describes the three attachment styles. I also liked some of the exercises in the book including the chart for reflecting on previous and current relationships and analyzing activating and deactivating strategies in which partners would engage. Plenty of easy-to-follow examples too. My 2 biggest struggles were was the lack of reflection on *how* a person could move to a more secure attachment style, and the seeming emphasis that the three styles are specifically distinct. To me, the avoidant-secure-anxious trichotomy feels like it should be a spectrum, as I myself have connected with behaviours in all three categories. But the author always refers in the examples to “X person has a Y attachment style”. Is their attachment style an intrinsic personality trait? Or is it a behaviour that can fluctuate? The author seems to infer the former and only goes so far as to say that secure partners make their partners more secure. But what I read was: secure = good, anything else = bad (and even goes so far as to remind you multiple times that according to research “most people are secure”, so if you find yourself in the anxious/avoidant category, sucks for you). Going back to the examples, they were clear but honestly kind of obvious sometimes, especially in the later chapter on effective communication. It seems like it was thrown in as a tip on how to be more secure, but doesn’t go into nuance of communication; most examples are kind of clearly exhibiting not just anxious/avoidant, but “rude” behaviours, you can easily spot that without understanding attachment styles. I can see how using these styles can help identify key issues in relationships and there are a few exercises I still intend to write for myself, but it felt like a point was made in chapter 1 and then I didn’t learn anything except how to be considerate toward your partner and recognize some red flags.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book was a great enlightenment for me , and I’m truly grateful for what I learned. It helped me understand a lot about myself and about intimate relationships.
