I will probably re-read, and I wish I’d read this before I started dating. Thinking of the person who owned this before me and used it to press a flower 🌼

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I read this book so I could spend my holiday diagnosing my friends (also trying to enjoy their holidays) as 'anxious', 'avoidant', etc. They found this insufferable, I fear, but I thought it was most entertaining. I will continue to say 'that's very avoidant of you' when my friends are unavailable for coffee for the foreseeable.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: As someone who is very obviously anxiously-avoidant, I found this super insightful. Wonderful wonderful wonderful introduction to attachment styles for those who have—or are involved with people who have—insecure ones. Also: “Our need for someone to share our lives with is part of our genetic makeup, and has nothing to do with how much we love ourselves and how fulfilled we feel on our own.” ….the part of the plot that western culture has sometimes lost.🤨

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This is a daily life book. I hope I come back to it frequently for check-ins when I'm feeling anxious. I particularly liked the section at the end as it put me to the test and proved that I still had more to learn about being secure. I used this book for friendships rather than romantic relationships and was disappointed that the book did not at all refer to other types of relationships that attachment theory could be helpful for. Otherwise, a solid read and one I will be recommending.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Interested in learning why you’re fucked up and entirely unlovable ? Read this book! Joking aside, this book was an excellent explanation of why couples with different attachment styles are destined to fail, and provides practical advice on how to work through common relationship pitfalls.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: It should be fashionable to read books like this to learn about love. Not from fictional literature or movies. We all know truth is stranger than fiction but how often do we take care to remember it? An essential read.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: A little repetitive but at least it gives you loads of examples. I feel like this should be mandatory literature for anyone who's getting romantically involved with anyone. You can tell it's a little outdated (granted, the research is already quite established) but still very valuable.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: The book was quite insightful how relationships work and you can find what type you are through this book and the psychology behind it, so that was super interesting. However, it was quite repetitive and quite long. I think it could have been 100 pages less. But overall a good one!

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: It’s a good start if you don’t understand attachment theories. But I felt like it just scratches the surface with some issues and does not take into individual complexities like trauma. Nevertheless I am really glad I picked it up.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: спасибо этой книге за то, что я проанализировала все свои предыдущие отношения и ВСЁ ПОНЯЛА ))) тут есть хорошие мысли. а есть очень натянутые идеи, которые не вяжутся с научпопом. поэтому вайбов тут больше от сэлф-хэлпа (но это ок — то что надо сейчас, когда я вообще не могу ничего читать)

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: An interesting insight into relationships and attachment styles, particularly useful for the dating world but really everyone can benefit. Helpful advice and generally agree but not ever a fan of books that want me to do worksheets throughout. 3.7

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book really applies to all types of relationships. Not just romantic ones. I found some of it too generalized. It's hard to filter everyone into one of three categories. But still gives some great insight into your relationships.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Would definitely recommend reading Attached - it's helped me understand my needs and what to be looking for in a partner. It also gives really good practical advice on how to be more securely attached which is stuff I will try to practice as a anxiously attached individual :‘)

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I read this one because we’ve been talking about it in therapy haha. I found it really helpful, so much so I wish i would’ve read this when I was dating! It helped me be a lot more self aware, and I enjoyed it!

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: If you’ve read a lot about attachment styles, this book isn’t anything new or revolutionary. (I’m a therapist whose graduate thesis involved attachment styles) That being said, I think this book would be really helpful for anyone who’s trying to develop a better understanding of their own attachment style and their partner’s attachment style. It’s tangible and practical.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: A lot to think about after listening to this. It was interesting how the majority of the secure examples all focused on talking about the issue as it came up. A good reminder to me to say how I feel when I feel it

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Outstanding and so easy to read. Even if you’re already married, this book comments on practical ways to calm your active attachment system and tools for identifying if you have attachment wounds. I would recommend this book to anyone who is dating, looking, engaged, or married. Their perspective on attachment in relationships is an important read.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I knew quite a bit of the stuff included before reading the book but it is good to revise these things. Also, there are practical guides that help you work with your attachment style and communicate with people with other styles. Short, to the point, recommended.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: feels weird to rate this book so low when it was legitimately so helpful for me. i just can't baseline recommend it, it feels catered to a very specific personality type (which happens to be mine). i dont know that it functions fully as an unbiased educational resource, which is what i feel like it's trying to be

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Not bad voor een "zelfhulpboek" over de liefde. Ik onthoud: liefde alleen is meestal niet genoeg, de meesten onder ons moeten leren hoe we het beste een team vormen in de liefde <3 Goed nieuws, het is allesbehalve onmogelijk en dit boek kan je wel een zetje geven :)

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This was a super insightful and informative read about relationships and the dynamics between the people in them. This can be for people looking for love, in a relationship or even aspects of family relationships and friendships. Really good on audio!

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Truly a fantastic book and a must read for anyone. Taught me way more than I expected about myself and my attachment type, as well as how this will interact with other attachment types. And what I should look for in a partner and what patterns of behavior I’m prone to fall into. And most importantly, how to pursue and maintain a healthy attachment and conflict resolution.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: i enjoyed reading a deep dive into attachment theory and seeing it in practice through vignettes. it was interesting to apply the theory to my own relationship and engage in the exercises included in the book! definitely made me think about attachment differently.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: BIG fan! Have already recommended to many clients. I think the knowledge they present can help with any relationship, and found it especially interesting that the book covered the three types of attachment rather than focusing on one to give a full spectrum view and help people understand themselves and others.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book really supports people with unhealthy attachment styles to recover and transform them into a safe one. Lots of stories, exercises and easy to follow steps make this book a real transformative journey. It can trigger your past and might make you feel deeply, but I guess the point is in self-realisation and healing. Really recommend it to everyone who seeks change in their relationships patterns. Thank you.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: 2 cancelled flights gave me the time to binge read this therapist-recommended gem. I wish I read this years ago. Very helpful and accessible read for learning about secure relationships with some practical exercises included for personal reflection and application of the concepts discussed.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I didn’t know how much I would get out of it since me and pookie are both secure but I loved it - some of the studies were SO cute and made me feel mushy and I feel like I gained a lot of insight that I will be thinking about when I’m talking to my friends about their sitchs

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Appreciate it as far as relationship help books go, enjoyed the research element the narrative is built on as well as the practical applications provided. However a lot of concepts feel like they need a refresh and it feels there is too much focus on the anxious! Would have liked to learn more about the nuances between the different attachment types.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I wish I had read this book in my 20s. Highly recommended for folks who are dating—but it’s just as valuable for people in committed relationships. I found it extremely beneficial for my marriage. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Interesting read on the theory of adult attachments in romantic relationships. While the categorisation of every human relationship into 3 categories of Secure (50% of the population), Anxious (21%), and Avoidant (25%) may not be all inclusive and exhaustive for those with a discerning and scrutinising disposition; however, it does offer a useful insight into your relationships, if you can relate to one of the 3 categories. What I liked about the book is that it doesn't tell you which is the best category to belong to, or how you should change in order to be more Secure (the category ideally suited for all relationships - the O Negative of relationships). The lessons in the book are more about understanding the 3 categories and feeling comfortable with yours in order to avoid the negative emotions that come associated with relationships between people belonging to different categories; especially ones that arise from Anxious-Avoidant relationships, which tends to happen most frequently despite the inherent incompatibilities. Given their nature, this book is more likely to be read by people belonging to the Anxious category, and much less by the Avoidants, who could possibly benefit the most from it.

It clearly delivers on the hope that the authors have for this book: “We hope that you will use the relationship wisdom distilled in this book, from more than two decades of research, to find happiness in your romantic connections and to soar in all aspects of your life. If you follow the attachment principles we have outlined, you will be actively giving yourself the best shot at finding—and keeping—a deeply gratifying love, instead of leaving one of the most important aspects of your life to chance!” (pp. 272-273) Based on the science of attachment, the book looks at the three basic types of attachment: avoidant, anxious, and secure. In a nutshell: if you’re avoidant, relationships feel like a threat to your independence; if you’re anxious, relationships feel like a lifeline that is going to be yanked away from you at any moment; if you’re secure, relationships provide you with peace of mind. Early on, the book helps you determine your style of attachment, and the style of your partner as well. After helping to determine attachment styles, the book takes a closer look at how these three different attachment styles present themselves in everyday life, and when they are most likely to clash. Not surprisingly, the most clash-likely relationship is between a person with an avoidant style of attachment and one with an anxious style. (Can we say distancer and pursuer?) The authors provide both insight and hope for helping avoiding the needless suffering often accompanying this attachment style mis-match: “People have very different capacities for intimacy. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Approximately the first 70 pages could be rated ~3 stars as they give an overview of the attachment concept and introduce the attachment types. Mostly handy for those who have never heard of it or have little knowledge in the field. A little quiz may help someone to better understand how certain behaviors stem from a specific attachment style. After those 70 pages one should close the book and stop reading it right there. I'm really surprised how deceitful the high rating in Goodreads and this superb annotation of the book are in comparison to the content of the book after the first 70 pages or so. In my view, it could do more damage than good for those with little self-awareness, critical thinking or knowledge in the field. Now when I was looking through some reviews I can agree with Melinda that probably 5 stars rating for this book comes from anxiously attached people. As Melinda says "The authors are very sympathetic towards anxious types who are portrayed as victims throughout the whole book while avoidant types are portrayed as cold, selfish, and abusive." and I have the same impression. That's one thing I disliked. Sketchy examples and case studies. Interpretation of some seems to be tweaked to present what the authors want. Attachment is definitely not the most salient issue in some. Proposed solution to all insecure types is just to find a secure partner. Like a secure partner will be your ultimate rehab. Yes, no trace of thought that 'hey, perhaps you also need to look deeper into your attachment issues'. The book mainly carries on with the premise 'So you have needs, it's fine, you are fine; just go and find yourself a securely attached partner; he/she will fix it for you. Oh, and make sure to keep the securely attached one! (in case you did not get that for the multiple times we already stated it)'.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: While sharing the occasional snippet of relationship wisdom, this book far from delivers what I hoped for. It is full of rhetorical questions and long introductions that waste the readers time (have you ever heard of citation? Or APA style? Footnotes?). Additionally, it makes people's relationships out to be nothing more than a reflection of one of three (or four) attachment styles - which, by the way, means that no one has a "unique" attachment style. Much of the book reads more like a Cosmopolitan quiz than a pop psychology book based on the latest studies in adult attachment. The "unique" attachment styles that are described are posed as the sole indicator of whether a relationship will succeed or fail. The authors presume that any action someone takes is indicative of their attachment style and not possibly of their current situation. There are too many blanket statements and subtle judgments about the "insecures" being less-than. An actual excerpt: "Before we learned about attachment theory, we took the secures of the world for granted, and even dismissed them as boring. But looking through the attachment prism, we've come to appreciate secure people's talents and abilities. The goofy Homer Simpson-like colleague whome we barely noticed was suddenly transformed into a guy with impressive relationship talent who treats his wife admirably, and our get-a-life neighbor suddenly became a perceptive, caring person who keeps the entire family emotionally in check. But not all secure people are homebodies or goofy. You are not settling by going secure! Secures come in all shapes and forms. Many are good-looking and sexy. Whether plain or gorgeous, we've learned to appreciate them all for what they really are - the "super-mates" of evolution - and we hope that you will too." ... anyone who think Homer Simpson is in any way an ideal relationship role model has never watched the Simpsons and is delivering inaccurate relationship advise... Also, "super-mates"?!?!?! I find

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I read this book immediately following "Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents" and it did not hold up in light of what felt like a revelatory examination of emotional maturity and relationships. A few things irritated me as I read this book. First, it's extremely heteronormative; all relationships examples given in the book were between straight, cis couples, and secondly, in my opinion most were stereotypical in their portrayal of the kinds of problems experienced between men and women. This book has been recommended to me by several people, but I felt alienated by it. The three categories--anxious, avoidant, and secure--all felt too general. The behavior that was assigned into each of these three felt at times that it needed to be examined in a more nuanced way. Some behavior mentioned felt like it bordered on abusive and wasn't just an "attachment style". Also the advice seems to generally be "find someone mature to partner with who will put up with your bullshit, and maybe get better at communicating" which seems a little unfair to all those emotionally mature people out there. It's not their job to heal the rest of us.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Wasn't quite what I was expecting, there was less science and more practical advice. I don't think I got as much out of it as some people might (omg if you actually try to make your partner jealous and you are not in middle school, read this book asap), but I think the overall framework they presented is a useful concept. By classifying folks as anxious, secure and avoidant and not attaching any value judgments to those relationship styles, I think that is helpful for everyone. Sort of like how recognizing that there are introverts, extroverts and more balanced people means not using one to measure the worth of the others; they are just different ways of being. (And one of the things I appreciated was that the book noted that there is no correlation between relationship style and introversion; introverts can have secure attachment styles.) The thing I personally liked most was the idea of a partner providing a "secure base." I always function better when I have a partner; it makes me feel more able to go off and do things. It always seemed irrational, if the partner is not doing these things with me, why should it matter if I have someone to go home to? But they provide evidence that this is just how we're wired and having that security does make us more able to explore the world independently. Cool. But the best part is that it acknowledges that humans do need connection and there's nothing shameful about that. Complete self-sufficiency is sometimes promoted as the ideal, but that doesn't mesh with the reality of what humans need.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: [UPDATE: Just read Wired for Love instead. It portrays the three types with much more balance, intelligence, psychological insight and sympathy -- as well as being much shorter and less fluff. Much more compassion for 'avoidant' types. If you're the anxious type, Attached might be worth a look too: gives reassurance and more information and tips tailored to you.] Goes into great detail about anxious attachment, but hardly anything for helping avoidant types. It sets itself up claiming there are just three *styles*, but then the entire book is spent on how great secures are and how bad avoidants are. As other reviewers have said, it portrays avoidants as the villain and anxious as the victim. It briefly mentions the problems avoidants have (like the fact they find intimacy or attachment distressing/difficult, despite wanting it; that they repress feelings and can sometimes only access them when distracted; that they find it difficult to communicate their needs; etc.), but then it doesn't spend much time on how to overcome these problems. So, book is interesting but severely lacking. It should really be called 'Anxious Attachment: How To Be Treated Like Royalty When You're Prone To Freaking Out'.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: It was a interesting and thought-provoking book. However, it's very simplistic and basically says the solution is to date a secure partner and then everything will be fine. Unless you already are secure, and then you can date almost anyone and everything will be fine. I don't think things are ever that neat. Also, a weird omission was that they never talked about a partnership with two anxious style people. They at least mention a few times that two avoidant people rarely get together and why, which explained why they didn't talk about that pairing, but not a single word about anxious-anxious relationships. Why would those be unlikely to form? Would that be a disaster, or could it be better because both people understand what the other needs and why they act out, and be better at supporting each other than other relationship styles? I think this book is a good start, but I'd like to read a book that goes into more complicated situations as opposed to this book's simple views and situations.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Attached is about the science of adult attachment, in the context of love and relationships. Authors Amir Levine and Rachel Heller dive into attachment theory and three behavior styles: Anxious, Avoidant, and Secure. The book details each of these relationship styles, how to identify your own, and provides suggestions on how to best engage with each. ⁣ ⁣ I found myself agreeing with a lot, but not all, of the information in this book. I also found myself thinking about my own attachment style and how it’s changed over time. Attached was interesting to listen to and offers a lot to think about — 3.5 stars

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Not a single gay or bisexual story (meaning major case study) in a book about adult romantic relationships? Shame on the authors. What a turnoff. I also noticed a significant bias in favor of cases of single people. And of relationships lasting 10 years or less. This is a book aimed at single readers in their early 20s who can't find a decent date. Finally, the elephant in the room: diagnosis bias in favor of one "style" over the others. Sorry to ruin the suspense, but the authors much prefer the securely attached. I'm quite sure that more than half the population is quite chuffed to be labeled "secure." And after reading this book, they will "learn" only to date themselves. Racial purity achieved! While that other half, labeled "anxious" or "avoidant," can probably smell the whiff of pathology being sprayed in their direction. Why sell such ugly labels if the goal really is effective therapy? Don't modern metastudies (See my review of The Triumph of Experience) also claim that positivity is crucial to optimal mental health and wellbeing? Or maybe fear and loathing really do sell books, just like they sell news. I wanted to learn from this book, but as a woman married for 20 years to a woman who is also the mother of my child...whom we actually raised on the principles of attachment theory (!) um... not a lot for me to take away. Sadly I've had this complaint before about books in this genre. The gaping holes in the studies become unavoidable to readers whose basic experiences disprove the universal claims. For instance, a book on the same topic that I quite liked, A General Theory of Love, claimed universality but failed to account for adoption when defining the critical term "mother." As I saw instantly, being an adoptee. Unfortunately, reading this book with its Hetero biases so easy to see, one is reminded of how psychology has been used to tout norms and exert social control for centuries. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Unscientific and biased toward those with an anxious attachment style. Does not account for dangerous or abusive behaviors within either attachement style and makes out avoidance to be the problem that can easily fix an anxious partner if they only meet them in the middle. This is not the case in abusive relationships with an abusive anxious partner. This book is unscientific, simplistic and dangerous. I am a therapist and an addiction therapist.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I don't even know how to express how life-changing this book was/is for me. I read it in two days, devoured it. I think every person on earth should read this book, it would make all relationships and interactions better, giving us all a common language to use to talk about how we act, what we fear and what we need. I'm starting to put the lessons into practice, and it's scary. Terrifying! But, I know I'm on the right path and with lots of practice and a little time, I'll be successfully managing relationships with my best interests in mind. Please read this book! Especially if you have struggled in unhealthy relationships, find yourself running away from great people, or find yourself compromising everything you want to keep a runner around. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Leave aside for a second that "Attached" by Amir Levine and Rachel Heller slots everyone into 3 relationship attachment categories: secure (50% of the population), anxious (25%), and avoidant (25%) (I'm as suspicious of GUT paradigms as the next wannabe scientist). However, the authors are both experienced and practicing psychotherapists, and use case after case to provocatively and persuasively put forth their theory, and explain how recognising your own category (and/or sub category) can help you in your love life, whether you're single or coupled up. Leave aside as well that the examples are overwhelmingly heterosexual (I think I only read about one (tragic) gay couple): the situations, perceptions, strategies, manipulations, reactions, and aftermaths - all of it - can be translated into just about any kind of relationship. I was startled to see so many aspects of my various relationships over the years (and their breakdowns) described, but most shocking was my realisation that though I think I'm basically secure, I exhibit far more anxious characteristics than I knew or have ever admitted to myself before. What was nice was how unjudgmental the authors were of each category. There's little to criticise with the secure personality, but the anxious and avoidants were treated with compassion and courtesy, and especially fascinating were the explanations given for why there might be a preponderance of avoidants in the dating pool (they keep breaking up and re-circulating), and why the anxious-avoidant combo is common - despite their inherent incompatibilities (the vicious confirmation of worst expectations). And as someone who is beholden to telling the truth sooner, I was glad to see this injunction repeated throughout - be honest and upfront (to yourself and your lovers) about who you are and what you want and need. "Attached" is an easy read. I started and finished it on a cross-country flight. It's poppy but not pandering, and it's compelling enough to make you

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I'm a little embarrassed to admit that I read this. Not because it wasn't good, but because I have this thing about posting relationship-y self-help books on here. I don't want people to know that I spend time thinking about my relationship status. I want to seem cooler than that. However, I recently found myself dating a person who had me absolutely flummoxed. A friend suggested this book to me thinking it might offer some insight, and I read it rather quickly. This book is better than most relationship books I have read. The author describes how attachment theory can be applied to romantic relationships. There are three types of attachment: secure, anxious, and avoidant. According to the authors, 50% of the population is securely attached, 25% is anxious, and 25% avoidant. Luckily for me, I am anxious. Which is so much fun. The guy I was dating? Avoidant. Apparently this is the worst combination ever. Most of the book seems to focus on the pitfalls of this particular combination. Or maybe that's just what I chose to focus on. Anyway, I liked this book because I felt like it really helped me understand why this relationship wasn't working the way I wanted it to. The book provides a lot of examples and checklists and inventories so that you can figure out what's going on in your relationship, how you might be exacerbating the problems, and give suggestions about how you could respond instead. One thing I liked about this book is that the authors didn't suggest that we should all go around acting uninterested and like we don't want serious relationships when we do. This is the prevailing wisdom of most dating books out there. But, as the authors point out, this makes no sense, especially if you are anxiously attached. By pretending that you don't care about being in a serious relationship, you are just attracting the wrong people for you (avoidants, if you are anxious). Hooray for honesty!

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Looks fascinating, and I really want to read it, but it can't be renewed any more. ... Picked the book up to take it back to the library and got completely sucked in. Finished with two days to spare! This book proposes to explain the recurrent relationship disaster I've reenacted for most of my life ( with 1.5 exceptions). The idea is that there are basically three attachment styles, much like the styles babies have of attaching to their mothers: anxious, secure, and avoidant. The authors propose this as a 2-d graph sort of thing with four quadrants, but it seems more like one spectrum to me. Secure people are basically resilient, communicate clearly, trust each other, and develop emotional intimacy naturally. Avoidant people need a lot of space; if things get too intimate for them, they pull away. Anxious people easily get worried about the relationship and need a lot of closeness and reassurance. They can have great relationships and become more secure if they get that, but if they don't, they end up in a self-reinforcing biological spazz, much like the hot amygdala effect: the attachment system gets hypersensitive, and the braking systems of rationality get weakened. Unfortunately, avoidant and anxious people tend to be attracted to each other because they each reinforce the other's existing worldviews about relationships. Do this enough, and you can actually start thinking the misery dance that results from these conflicting styles is what passion feels like. Argh! (Sounds like a biological explanation for the love potion.) Main advice: be real from the beginning, quickly rule out anyone whose attachment style is too far from secure, and communicate your needs like a secure person would. One thing I would have liked to see (and maybe it was in there but I missed it): what happens if two anxious people get together? Do they reassure each other so much that they morph into a secure relationship, or do they do an f'd-up dance and end up making each other miserable?

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Wow this book literally dragged me. It allowed me to see where past relationships went wrong, ways that I can heal, and also affirmed my current relationship/dating choices. My therapist recommended this to me, and I honestly urge everyone to read this book. I really liked how this book made me aware of the patterns I have, because now I have the opportunity to work on myself in current relationship. The only thing is that this book is very cis/het. Everything is phrased as "his/her" and there was ONE SHORT example of an LGBTQ couple. Other than that, this book was so helpful and right on time.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Quite a disappointment. Having read this for a friend whom we'll call "Pristina", I noticed quite quickly that Attached is heavily biased against Avoidants (as many other reviewers have pointed out), wholly sympathetic to those who are Anxious, seem to revere those who are Secure, and do very little to actually help any of these attachment styles to become more secure themselves. Why is this problematic. Yes, it's tragic that those who are Anxious came from a family with whom were inconsistent in their care and love but it's no less tragic than a child who grows up to be dismissive or fearful avoidant due to neglect, narcissistic parenting, or a parent(s) suffering from addiction(s). The point shouldn't be only about sympathesising (only the Anxious style) but also about the fact that trauma can be unlearned through self and personal growth. Okay, so I admit there is a section that does somewhat talk about how to unlearn trauma by learning to be more Secure but the way they advise to be more Secure is, I think, highly toxic and immature -- get together with someone who is Secure. Basically, if you're a big trauma-mess, find someone to fix you. That's terrible advice. Other niggles: - Too many anecdotes that seem far-fetched and placate too much to romantic tropes. As these stories don't have any citations, it's hard to take these scenarios as anything other than imperfect examples. This way of defining the problem by way of pretending that a story can speak to human experience is a false equivalence fallacy and therefore, to put it bluntly, is ludicrous. - No direct citations. Few listed works in the bibliography. Attachment Theory was not in its infancy when this book was written so I'm at a loss as to why the authors found it not useful to use the research as part and parcel to their arguments. - Not all Secures come from Happy Families. review_body: This is what I get for not properly vetting my interlibrary loan requests. And I'm reminded of Sally telling Harry (in the movie, the greatest, best movie) about how after dinner, her date reached over, plucked a hair out of her head, and started flossing with it. Honestly, I half expect that shit to happen at this point. Dating is terrible. Anyway. Things I already knew: I'm pretty good at communication! People open up to me! It's nice! I'm securely attached! But before my self-congratulations go too far, like most women in our culture, I have anxious tendencies. And since most dudes in our culture (even the securely attached ones!) have avoidant tendencies, like, there's the conflict, or something. I didn't learn anything new there that I didn't already know from (a) life and (b) friends who are smarter (and better researched in this area) than me. So check out this book if you think you should, and don't if you don't. Trust me, I

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: In a culture that scorns dependence and exalts self-reliance, Levine and Heller make the argument for the Dependency Paradox—that the more effectively dependent people are on one another in their inner circle, the more independent and daring they become in the greater world. Or the opposite of Kanye’s central thesis in The Life of Pablo. The basic premise of Attached is to challenge present-day thinking that dependence is weak and that mastering and controlling our emotions is strong. Not only is effective dependency healthy, but in a secure union, it actually makes the dependents more individually effective than they otherwise would have been on their own. The book then covers the three most common attachment types—avoidant, anxious and secure—and how to form a secure union among people with different attachment types (hint: secure is best). Basic overview is that secure people feel comfortable with intimacy and are warm and loving, anxious people crave intimacy and are preoccupied with their relationships, and avoidant people equate intimacy with a loss of independence and constantly try to minimize closeness. Best quote: People are only as needy as their unmet needs.

review_body: Okay, so I understand that the title is EXTREMELY cheesy and I feel a teensy bit embarrassed to have read this. BUT, HEAR ME OUT because I'm not kidding when I say that this has been one of my most enlightening reads of the past few years (or maybe I'm just trying to justify to myself that this was worth reading, we shall never know). I've always found the concept of "attachment styles" quite fascinating. While I've read articles here and there on this topic, I wanted a more in-depth understanding of how it all works. I'm glad I picked up this book in particular because it not only very lucidly explains the functioning of these styles, but also manages to help you gain immense insight into how you, as an individual, function. This insight truly aids you in navigating through your relationships (be it romantic or platonic) in a better and a less conflicting manner. "Attached", in a nutshell, delineates how attachment styles - anxious, avoidant and secure, react when they are in a relationship. The authors not only focus on the individual styles, but also study the styles when they are in concert with each other. The language is simplistic and multiple examples are cited to make the readers come face-to-face with possible situations that may arise in our own lives. In all these scenarios, the authors tell their readers that the one thing which remains paramount is our peace and happiness, and one must consciously make decisions as to what kind of people we wish to surround ourselves with. In this context, by helping you to recognize your personal attachment style, the authors also help you to recognize others' attachment styles so that you can accordingly make the choice as to whether you want such people around you who fail to understand not only their own needs, but also yours. review_body: I've struggled to review this book. I feel somewhat bad for giving it such a low rating. I understand how this book can be really helpful and I don't want to rain on that parade. It is a relief to be told that there is nothing wrong with us for wanting close intimate connection. I am completely behind Levine when he tells us that we all deserve to be treated with respect and dignity by our romantic partners. That's a great message, but it's one that doesn't require science to be effectively delivered. It is the science part of this book that I take issue with. Here is a list of what bothers me the most: 1. Levine's view of attachment theory seems to be half baked. I read the whole book and I still don't understand what he was getting at. He doesn't present much science at all and prefers anecdotes, which just aren't cutting it for a book proclaiming that it is based on 'new science'. I ended up feeling like he had taken a somewhat interesting psychological theory and spun it into a popular self-help framework without preserving any scientific integrity. Levine is altogether too sure that he is speaking for 'science'. I am skeptical of anyone making such claims. 2. Levine tells us that we are all categorized into three 'attachment styles' (anxious, avoidant, and secure). Then he tells us that attachment styles are 'plastic, not fixed', meaning they can change. I am confused, what is the point of the groups then? Why not observe human behavior in relationships without attempting to categorize people by it? We are not entirely defined by our behavior, especially if we can control and change our behavior, are we? 3. Levine tells us that each 'attachment style' has different attachment needs and that therefore we are not all compatible with each other. I do not agree with this - whatever our attachment style is we all desire love and intimacy in fundamentally similar ways. Furthermore, he makes the case that those with an avoidant attachment style are unsuitable 'mates'.

review_body: One of the more insightful self-help books about relationships I have come across, and I've been thinking about it a lot since I finished. Basically, the book gives you a kind of conceptual framework for thinking about how different people approach romantic attachment, and categorizes people's relationship behavior as either anxious, avoidant, or secure. The secure people are comfortable with intimacy and are usually warm and loving, while anxious people crave intimacy and worry about their partner's ability to love them back, and avoidant people try to minimize closeness and worry about losing their independence. It may be a bit of an oversimplification, but the concepts are still really useful since they provide a pretty compelling explanation of why some relationships turn toxic and some are healthy and nurturing. I like how the book not only gives a good explanation of where things go wrong, especially in relationships where one person is anxious and the other avoidant, but also gives a lot of positive examples of what works in relationships and where things go right. There's solid discussion of when and how to end an unsatisfying relationship, as well as of ways to try to bring a relationship between one or more insecure partners into a more secure and mutually satisfying place. The writing is clear and easy to understand without feeling dumbed down. The authors mention at some points that attachment styles are malleable, and we can change over time and go from having a secure attachment style to an insecure one, and vice versa, based on life events and relationship experiences. It would have been interesting to have deeper discussion of this, and the degree to which the attachment styles are a continuum or varying spectrum versus cut-and-dried categories. I recognized past and current parts of myself in the descriptions of each of the three styles. It's written for the average layman, and therefore goes lighter on the footnotes (though the bibliography at the end was useful). It also contains helpful worksheets for the reader to assess themselves, and helpful suggestions for the reader to improve. The Secure type (most common), the Anxious type (needs reassurance/intimacy), and the Avoidant type (runs away from intimacy). The Anxious-Avoidant relationship is the most common: the anxious person will chase for reassurance, the avoidant will avoid the intimacy, and when the relationship ends, the anxious person will say: yes, there is something wrong with me for wanting more intimacy (needy) and the avoidant will feel that justified in their belief that they are a strong, independent person. But underlying the book is this (although it only comes out clearly in the conclusion): each person has different needs for intimacy. Some people will need more, some people will need less. The book addresses how you express your need for intimacy. I particularly liked that the book was not judgmental about people having different intimacy needs - but instead supported effective communication of these needs. I also liked that the book directly addressed the avoidant: It's simply more socially acceptable to maintain a cool, self-sufficient facade. So they hide their wishes and mask their discontent. Here's why: 1) Attachment Style Tests: The inclusion of tests to identify one's own and their partner's attachment styles adds a practical dimension to the book. These assessments enhance self-awareness and contribute to a deeper understanding of relationship dynamics. 2) Practical Exercises: The book goes beyond theory, providing readers with practical exercises. These exercises facilitate a better grasp of attachment styles in interpersonal communication, aiding individuals in navigating and comprehending potential partners more effectively. 3) Communication Examples: By offering real-life communication examples, the book assists in establishing secure foundations for both avoidant and anxious partners. This practical guidance proves invaluable for readers seeking to enhance their relational dynamics. 4) Biological Mechanisms: Exploring the biological mechanisms underpinning relationship needs adds a scientific perspective. The book effectively breaks down these mechanisms, enhancing readers' comprehension of the psychological aspects influencing attachment styles. 5) Everyday Application: The book seamlessly integrates theory with practicality, illustrating how day-to-day conversations and conflicts serve as manifestations of the attachment system. This real-world application makes the content relatable and applicable to readers' own experiences. This book is particularly beneficial for those interested in building meaningful relationships. It may not resonate well with individuals unsure of their relationship goals or those who question the necessity of a committed partnership. review_body: Confession--I actually like to read relationship books, but I'm always rather hesitant to rate and review them on Goodreads. I guess it feels just a little too cheesy to me, but truly I am a cheesy kind of person at times! Additionally, if relationship books are research-based and well-written, I think more of us SHOULD read them! After all, as the author's note, "Relationships are one of the most rewarding of human experiences--above and beyond other gifts that life has to offer...But despite the importance we assign to our most intimate bonds, most of us still know very little about the science behind romantic relationships, and allow ourselves to be guided all too often my misconceptions and myths." Now that I have that out of the way--This was a great book! According to Levine and Heller's research, similar to attachment theory principles governing childhood development, adults also have attachment styles that affect their actions and reactions in relationships. There are secure, avoidant and anxious attachment styles. This book helped me understand myself in some very important ways, and to better understand previous relationships I've been in more clearly. Respond sensitively to their distress. Check in with them from time to time. Provide comfort when things go wrong. Don't interfere. Provide behind the scenes support for their endeavors. review_body: Bit of a cheesy title but a great book for those of us who are mildly anxiously attached :D A 'tl:dr' for the whole text could be: "If you want to take the road to independence and happiness, first find the right person to depend on and travel down it with them." Very study-and-evidence-based writing, that is still accessible to the non-psychologists of the world. I like the fact that it goes against the popular relationship advice narrative of "you are responsible for how you feel, irrespective of your partners' behavior". Who we love is one of the most important decisions we make in our lives, and one that is directly correlated with how we will feel in our bodies and in most areas of our life, for a vast majority of the time - there's no need to pretend that that's not true. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Wow, this book made me realize that people fall into 3 categories: secure, anxious, and avoidant. There's no such thing as a bad relationship, it all boils down from your childhood to past experiences that made you do things. I would recommend this book to someone in a relationship or thinking of getting into a relationship. This book gave me an early insight on how to mitigate fights in a relationship. It also gave me other perspectives to look into to better understand other people.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: There is some interesting information in this book. That said, it's heavily skewed to favor anxious attachers over avoidant ones, and contains little of value for the fearful-disorganized type. There are articles on the web, blog posts, and YouTube videos that cover most of the topics in this book better. As an example of what I mean, at one point, the authors claim that it is simple and easy to soothe an anxious attacher, and that if you do, you will be rewarded with a very devoted partner. This is not universally true. Some anxious attachers are impossible to soothe, and thus never emerge from their fear response, meaning they remain wholly self-centered in relationships. Also, the constant harassment, gaslighting, and cruel judgments anxious attachers are prone to hurling at their partners when escalated can be just as damaging as the distancing tactics of the avoidant type. The overarching message to anxious attachers in this book is, "You're fine. You don't need to change or grow internally to become more secure. All your behavior is completely understandable. You just need to find a secure partner to soothe you." Meanwhile, avoidant attachers are condemned in this book. The authors all but scoff at the need for autonomy, and proclaim that avoidant attachers must change their thinking about dependency and learn to take responsibility for the feelings of others. Avoidant attachers are figured as the villains in many of the case studies. The overarching message is, "Your behavior is cruel and your thought patterns are harmful. You must change." On top of this, there is precisely and expressly zero help offered specifically to fearful disorganized attachers. The authors say this type is rare, so they should just read everything in the book. The overarching message here is, "You're too weird for us to bother with. You're on your own." For my part, I think that humans have needs for both autonomy and closeness. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: By clearly sketching different relationship types, this book is able to classify well-known patterns many partners struggle with or have struggle with. The problem with these patterns is that they are static, oversimplistic and thus miss the dynamic nuances that make all the differences. Instead of seing relationships as something where two people relate each other to the partner (that is: influence and are influenced by the partner), the book suggests that there is a static type in each of us. Even though this static approach is softened in some of the chapters, the main assumption is not questions nor put into context. I don't see how the attachment types offer a better mental model to explain relationship dynamics than a simple need-based model. However, this model adds another big flaw which makes the book almost dangerous: It is judgemental. Instead of putting the types next to each other and using them in a way to differentiate between needs, it strongly emphasizes with one of the three types ('anxious') but makes little effort to understand or emphasize with the needs of the other types. Instead, these are judged on the basis of how much they are fulfilling the anxious' partner's needs, nonewithstanding their own. This in not questionable from a scientific point of view but also stupid to toxic when it comes to supporting readers. People who have a stronger need for independence than closeness feel compelled by the book (see also other comments). For those falling into the anxious category, on the other side, the book gives little to no support to understand their partner's needs. Quite the opposite, it convicts their behavior and thus makes it even more difficult to open up. Instead of raising the idea that two people share responsibility for their partnership, this book burries it even further by reinforcing the victim-offender pattern that people have chosen for some reason or the other. review_body: Gimana rasanya punya partner yang bikin ngerasa aman & nyaman? It feels amazing. Going back & forth to therapist helps me to know myself more. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book was recommended to me, and I'm glad it was because, as a rule, I wouldn't go near anything with 'perfect match' in the title! This is a useful introduction to attachment theory and how it applies to adult relationships. It sheds some light on human behaviour in relationships and how we can get stuck in repeating patterns that make us and our partners unhappy... I know there is a large body of evidence on attachment but I couldn't comment on the evidence base for the authors' claims. It seems to explain an area of psychology in clear and practical terms though. It doesn't attribute absolutely everything to how your parents bonded with you as a baby, and it does advise on steps you can take to develop a more secure attachment style. All helpful for most adults, probably, whether in relationships or not, though it can feel a little simplistic at times. My main criticism of this book is that it could be confusing if your attachment style doesn't seem to fit neatly into one of the three categories - secure, anxious or avoidant. On the book's website, the authors reply to a question about this: "Only a very small percentage of the population falls into the fourth, combination, category (3-5%). On the other hand, LOTS of people think they fall into this category! [...] Another reason is that some of the anxious and avoidant behaviors are almost identical, so people can’t decide if they’re one or the other – and conclude that they’re both." They advise that people whose attachment style is mixed can benefit from reading the content directed at individuals in both the anxious and avoidant categories, and doing the exercises. I think that area needs to be explained a bit more though, given that the reader's understanding of their own attachment style is central to what they get from the book. 'Attached' took me ages to read because I left it and came back to it. I think it might be helpful to dip into now and again as a reminder.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: [11/10/15 review - later reviews follow] [Short version] if you spend time introspecting about patterns you or your partners have exhibited across many relationships, I believe this book could be a powerful lens with which to examine that history, as it has been for me. [Long version] I've known about childhood attachment theory for some time, but had not heard about the adult version until encountering this excellent book. Written in an entertaining and accessible style, it is nonetheless the work of scientists talking about peer-reviewed science, and has proper references for its claims, as well as helpful anecdotes from the authors' practices for illustration. If you're already familiar with attachment styles, you know about anxious and secure attachment in children; both are present in adult attachment, with the addition of avoidant attachment as a new archetype (at least to me). The book details the patterns of behavior of each type in a way that is surprisingly specific; most likely, as I did, you will see yourself and others you have been involved in fit (mostly) neatly into these attachment types. I think the book raises more questions than it answers, and its attempts at providing tools for bridging the attachment types seem a little too simplistic, but even seeing/thinking about/naming the patterns is powerful, in that by understanding the patterns we might be able to notice and thus stop the patterns from governing our behavior in the situations where it matters most. [12/16/18] Just read this for the second time; it's amazing how a few years of relationships with the perspective of this book has made me more aware of these patterns; still, reading it again made me notice a wealth of phenomena I had not noticed the first time, both in my own behaviors and in people I've had relationships with. Clearly this is a book I need to keep re-reading over and over again.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Atasamentul nu se naste si se opreste in prima copilarie, ci ne marcheaza relatiile de cuplu adulte in aceeasi maniera in care ne-a marcat calitatea relatiei cu parintii si apoi cu mediul pe care am ales a-l explora. Atasamentul nu e un fir stabil din copilarie pana la maturitate - pe langa modelul parental, se pare ca exista o componenta genetica ce predispune spre formarea unor tipare anxioase sau evitante, sunt modificari ce apar in urma experientelor de cuplu adulte, deci e pana la urma ca mai tot in psihologie, un construct cu multiple surse de variatiune. Ceea ce mi s-a parut util: descrierile tipologice pt atasamentul anxios si evitant sunt utile pentru auto- si hetero'diagnosticare'; dificultatile ce apar in relatiile cuplurilor anxios-evitante sunt clar explicate; este stiintific infirmata toata cultura strategiilor de flirt, de gasire a partenerului prin jocuri si trickuri in favoarea comunicarii eficiente si a asumarii propriilor nevoi ca ghid de selectie, necesitand uneori mutarea pe 'mute' a sfaturilor priceputilor in dating (chiar si un atac destul de clar asupra culturii individualismului exagerat este formulata fara menajamente, ceea ce mi-a placut!). Mai putin util mi se pare faptul ca alti factori ce duc la succesul relational sunt prea putin explorati (comunicarea & rezolvarea de conflicte apar in capitolele finale, dar focusul e pe studii de caz si mie cel putin mi se par greu generalizabile/aplicabile indicatiile autorilor) ; ca asupra atasamentului securizant se insista cel mai putin (caci despre bine stim ca e greu sa scrii; ca daca atasamentul anxios inca pare a fi salvabil, fata de cel evitant mai ca aveam senzatia ca autorii nutresc o animozitate nestiintifica. O carte utila pt cei ce incearca sa isi inteleaga mai bine relatiile sau vor sa afle cum pot construi relatii mai satisfacatoare in viitor, pe axa ingredientului atasament. Pentru alte ingrediente voi cauta si alte carti :)).

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: oh WOW do I hated this book. First, and foremost: the APPALLING lack of diversity. Don't expect this to look at any non-heterosexual relationships. Every single example is a man and a woman except for one gay couple who was mentioned for three sentences. That, by itself, feels like it would alienate most readers. Then there's the names -- every single person in this book has a stereotypically white name, making the examples unrelatable, and encouraging the mainstream mentality that the only people who can work on their relationships are white middle-class people. Also, though the authors say that the roles one plays in a relationship aren't about gender, almost every example of an anxious person is a woman, and every avoidant person is a man. Also, every secure person is a man. It only highlights existing, socially-accepted disparities between the sexes in relationships, and not acknowledging that gender roles have a role to play here is terrible and harmful to the entire argument. Finally, the pronouns were always he or she or s/he, which is also reductive. Finally, as someone with an avoidant style, I learned nothing except the fact that I'm a bad partner. This doesn't feel like a productive conclusion, but there are absolutely no tips here for people who are avoidant, even if we very much want to improve. Everything was laid out to highlight the flaws of the avoidant person, while commending the anxious person. This feels unfair. I will not recommend this book to ANYONE, I ended it angry and sad that something so widely-read could be telling people that people with my attachment style are basically not worth dating, as every single example makes the avoidant partner out to be almost irreparably bad. Basically, this book is so poorly thought out I'm surprised it was published in this state.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Attachment theory is a fascinating area of research. I first heard of it while reading on Takeo Doi's concept of amae, the unconscious desire to depend on the people around oneself. Attachment theory helps to show how amae originates in the child-mother bond and ends up pervading the Japanese psyche. Similarly, child attachment theory is extended here to explain adult relationships with uncanny accuracy. "Attached" reads like a field manual for those navigating the dating scene, but it's actually more than that. One can use this to make sense of tensions in an otherwise stable marriage, a falling out between friends and even workplace dynamics. Although most of the points tend to be obvious to a secure type, there are enough a-ha moments to make this worth reading. Moreover, the book has plenty of real life examples to guide the reader through the concepts and to drive some important lessons home. Recommended.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: It’s always difficult to fully believe anything that supposes all of human behavior can be strictly categorized but I believe these types are each meant to be viewed as a spectrum. I also believe someone can be somewhat fluid in their type. Either way it doesn’t matter much because I agree with a lot of what is said and at the very least this is all great advice on how to view attachments. I also just think it’s a good thing for people to analyze the concept of attachment and how that influences their behavior in relationships.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Do humanity a service and throw this book in the trash. It got off the wrong chapter and verse with its dustjacket endorsement from John Gray, author of the worthless Mars/Venus series. The only thing good about this book is introducing attachment theory (and that wasn't an original insight uncovered by the authors). Learning that I was someone with an anxious attachment style, helped me understand that I did't have to beat myself up when I suffer the consequences of getting overly attached to people, or when I have to overcompensate in the other direction. That's just the way I am, and I'm doing the best to change it. The book makes the claim that everybody has the right to have their emotional needs met. The problem with this is that if you're anxious, just about everything will make you feel insecure. So if you're needy all the time, are you going to say to your lover, "Honey, this makes me feel insecure," "Honey, this makes me jealous," "Honey, I think you need to spend more time with me"? Like people owe you that attention. Even if you say it diplomatically. Yeah OK, that's not gonna drive your lover away. I guess if you need to voice your concerns to your lover in order to avert passive-aggressive protest behavior, then do it. I don't have that problem. Just suck it up until you learn not to be that way anymore. If your secure partner is downstairs talking to another guy for two hours, just be patient and wait until she comes up so you can have your moment. This guy has an agenda, he just wants anxious people to break up with avoidants. I have no patience with these books encouraging neediness. Just grow a pair.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: As an unmarried woman of a certain age, I have continually struggled with relationships that have not lived up to my expectations. Either he was married to his work, married in real life, or wanted to marry me on the first date. I usually wanted more affection and attention than he wanted to give me (no matter who he was), and for a good decade or so, I thought this was all about him. I've been doing a lot of work on me recently, and have landed into the best relationship of my life. Of course I thought that because this particular man loves my face off, he would give me all the attention and affection I've been looking for all along. But it turns out that he, too, has times when what I want from him is too much. When he needs to be alone. When I overwhelm him. If any of this sounds even remotely familiar (or you identify with the men I've dated instead of me), this book can really help. It looks at attachment theory, and what that leads us to expect from our close relationships. It showed me that I want what I want because of the way I'm wired, not because I'm defective in any way. And it gives me strategies to get more of what I want when working with fellas who aren't wired this way. My only complaint about this book is that it continually rings the doomsday bell about anxious and avoidant people getting into relationships with each other. Since that's where I am, I couldn't help but feel MORE anxious while reading the book. But it's been incredibly insightful and, with a little help from a professional, I already feel more empowered to make some changes in my style and get on with my love life.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: The premise of the book is that each person can be classified into one of three groups of attachment styles: Anxious (often preoccupied with their relationships and tend to worry about their partner's ability to love them back); Avoidant (equate intimacy with a loss of independence and constantly try to minimize closeness); and Secure (feel comfortable with intimacy and are usually warm and loving). Finding myself identifying with a lot of the Avoidant tendencies was revelatory and shed light on some areas in which I can improve, but was also difficult, as I feel the authors wrote with the slant of patronizing Anxious personalities, deifying Secures, and painting Avoidants as the mean heartbreakers. Alas, I digress. This is a really helpful read to figure out which personalities work best together, and which are like oil and water (psst...Anxious and Avoidants). I appreciated the sections that give advice to the A's on becoming more Secure, and feel some sense of relief to have finally figured out why I tend to want to bolt when I feel smothered. I may have only given it three stars, but this book's content has made a deep impact on me. I applied these ideas not only to romantic partnerships, but every arena of interpersonal relationships, and can see more clearly why certain things feel suffocating to me but not everyone (extended text conversations, phone calls when I'm not in the mood to talk, children with a constant need for attention). Maybe too much information about me shared, but who reads these reviews anyway? ;) Read it if you're interested and let me know what you think...

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book is a personification of: 'no matter what your style of attachment is, you are valid' and 'you are not desperate if you're anxious'. I think it is good that the authors are inclusive in regards to this. Other than that, the book features some interesting studies and gives plenty of examples of the attachment styles and misunderstandings that can arise from them. They also give examples of when it is good to end the relationship (in the last few chapters). I do not know exactly why - even after all of my sweet words - I gave this book three stars. It was informative, nothing was too complicated and it did not feel too repetitive. But, it yet feels like there was something missing. In the beginning, it was often stressed that attachment style is not synonymous with personality, causing the attachment styles to be seen as ways of thinking that cross an entire spectrum of humans. I do get that it should not be reduced to personality, but I do think it has a huge influence. The researchers did state that attachment style has origin in multiple factors - upbringing, biology and past relationships - but I do wonder if they do not gloss over too much on the biological and environmental factors. Another thing is that exactly because of the personality factor seeming a little bit glossed over, some attachment behaviors seemed a little bit the opposite of what the authors claimed, to me. But this might be nitpicking. The book did its job, I cannot deny that. It was not a boring read and it was not unscientific.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Might be best if you are actually having relationship troubles. Someone recommended this book to me and I thought this might be an interesting read. Unfortunately it seems to be geared towards people who are actually in a relationship. It's a straightforward look at the types of attachment styles and how people can best adjust, cope, etc. when in relationships with certain relationship styles. There are quizzes and workbook exercises to help the reader(s) discover/analyze their style and the style of their partner. While somewhat interesting to read, the information seemed to be regurgitated in different ways in different anecdotes. I got it already, this story isn't telling me anything new. It also did not quite work in taking the next step: what does one DO further? I realize there's only so much a single book can do, but it just felt more like of a primer rather than something that could really help. As I'm not actually looking for a relationship I also couldn't help but feel that I really wasn't the audience for it. I don't have a partner to assess so there quite a bit of the book that did not quite apply. But if you're in a relationship and am curious about attachment styles, this might be a good read. I got it from the library and that sounds about right. Maybe bargain bin if you want to fill in the quizzes/activities and need a reference.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I loved this book. It was recommended to me by a close friend and it blew me away. On the surface, this book's content came as no surprise to me. There are three types of attachment styles? Check. I'm an anxious attacher? Yup no surprise there. I attract avoidants who can't give me what I need? Sounds about right. What blew me away about this book was the following: It's not wrong or bad to have an anxious attachment style. We are only as needy as our unmet needs. I consider myself a self-aware person and in my 30 years of living it had never really occurred to me to think of accepting myself as being someone who will always have an anxious attachment style. I've always resisted, I've always assumed one day I would grow into an avoidant. I didn't realize how much self-loathing I had about this part of myself. Reading through so many examples was powerful and insightful. I felt less alone and more able to name the patterns of attachment that I have had and continue to have in my life. This book really asked me to think about whether or not I want to keep being in relationship with people who are avoidants and will fundamentally have difficulty in giving me what I need to feel secure in my relationships. I struggled with this book and imagine I will return to it again. A wonderful read for anyone who is interested in understanding their relationship habits and wanting to understand just what they need to be happy in relationship.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Attachment theory provides a great explanation for a lot of behaviors. Here it is packaged in a very easy to read format that you can apply to your self and your relationships. Remember that handsome friend who just can't find a relationship, but he says he really wants to get married and he can just picture what the perfect girl would be like? Well that is all just classic avoidant BS. Don't bother setting him up with your other friends until he learns to work on his distancing strategies. This book has questionnaires that you do yourself, or if you are like me, you can sit down with your spouse and do them together and have a fun time determining that you are both pretty secure, but one of you is more anxious and the other is more avoidant. Guess what? You are not stuck forever in the attachment style that you developed as a baby. You can become more secure by dating secure people and using effective communication strategies. This book provided some research data to back up all its claims. There are also a number of case examples used to illustrate the concepts, which I typically enjoy. The only reason I gave it four stars instead of five is it seemed a little too oversimplified and pop-psychology for me. There wasn't the moving story or beautiful turn of phrase that can be found in the work of Bessel Van Der Kolk. I am going to read more of his books. Also, I now want to read more about effective compassionate communication.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: It would be a lie to say that I didn’t read this book in order to better understand my own attachment style (at first I even felt triggered and attacked)! The book is insightful and for someone who’s interested in human psychology it can be fun to read. However I found the book very vague and repetitive at times. It also suggested that your attachment style is mainly based on your individual experiences and upbringing, where in fact can vary from relationship to relationship or other aspects of the relationship’s dynamic. Some chapters were entirely refuted by suggesting that the theories mentioned are not necessarily “fixed attributes” for people fitting into the attachment styles. Which made no sense since the book kinda worked as a guide to figure out which attachment style you have. I often sensed that it was too optimistic, implying that people should compromise in, what seemed like, a one sided relationship in order to avoid conflict - “they understand that they can choose to live a Sisyphean life of ongoing disappointment and frustration, one to which they will continuously fight a losing battle or they can change their expectations”. So, you either fight everyday to get your point proven or just accept your fate. Only in chapter 10 does it give examples of people who gathered the strength to leave the toxic cycle with some tips on how to better survive the breakup. 3/5 ⭐️⭐️⭐️
