review_body: In the chapter on anxious types, he writes: Instead of thinking how you can change yourself in order to please your partner, as so many relationship books advise, think: Can this person provide what I need in order to be happy? The emphasis is on the "self," right? You're concentrating only on your needs. In the next chapter -- on avoidant types -- he writes: Another problem with self-reliance is the “self” part. It forces you to ignore the needs of your partner and concentrate only on your own needs, shortchanging you of one of the most rewarding human experiences: It prevents you (and the person you love) from the joy of feeling part of something bigger than yourself. This is the exact opposite of what he said before. I also can't help but feel that the initial advice is just kinda shitty, especially on the extreme ends of the spectrum. If everyone is rejecting you all the time, there might be something seriously wrong with you -- and it's going to be awful and painful to fix, but that doesn't mean it doesn't need fixing. Think about the "nice guy" who bends to everyone's will because he's too afraid to be assertive, so he ends up with the wrong partner because he's too afraid of the confrontation of breaking up with her. review_body: The needs of people with avoidant attachment are slightly disproportionately dismissed whereas those of people with anxious attachment are reinforced and encouraged. It felt a bit black and white at times to claim that a constant need for connection and intimacy is not something to be questioned, and that the best thing for someone with an anxious attachment is to search for a securely attached person who can meet their all needs, rather than to also find other ways to feel secure in addition to through relationships. On the other side, I could see the argument about people with anxious and avoidant attachments being incompatible, but it made me wonder whether things are this black-and-white. It felt a bit like the book promotes the idea that needs are met all the time in good relationships, but I think in practice things are a bit more complicated than that. The chapter on conflict resolution was great! Also interesting that the narative seemed to be that people with an avoidant attachment are unhappy in relationships because of problems to do mostly with themselves whereas people with an anxious attachment are unhappy because others can't meet their 'needs'. Seems a bit like a double standard. Also avoidant seems to be a label sometimes put onto people who are just being assholes. The advice given for avoidant attachment regarding deactivating tendencies seemed legit and helpful to me. Similarly, the examples of protest behaviours in anxious attachment helped me think about things I could do differently. The attachment types are described as separate categories, but I would find it more helpful to think about them in terms of spectrums on which people can probably move a little bit. review_body: this book dives deep into the fascinating world of attachment theory and explains how our attachment styles- secure, anxious, or avoidant . drawing from psychology and neuroscience, the author unpack why some people naturally crave closeness and reassurance, why others tend to pull away when things get too intimate, and how a secure balance can create the foundation for healthier bonds. what makes this book so engaging is that it doesn’t just stay theoretical- it actually helps you identify your own attachment style as well as that of your partner (or even past partners). through example stories, real-life scenarios, and practical tools, the author show how these patterns play out in everyday interactions- whether it’s how quickly you respond to a text, how you handle conflict, or what makes you feel loved and safe. it’s a powerful reminder of how much of our adult behaviour is shaped by early experiences. the book shows how childhood dynamics like how caregivers responded to our needs, often carry forward into adulthood, influencing how we show up in love, friendships, and even workplace relationships. once you see the patterns, you can’t unsee them. i especially loved the way the book highlights signs to look out for, and how it doesn’t just stop at “this is who you are” but actually gives guidance on how to work toward a healthier, more secure style. it encourages breaking cycles of anxious clinging or avoidant distancing, and instead learning to communicate, set boundaries, and create bonds that feel stable and fulfilling. that said, i did feel the book leaned a bit biased at times. while the focus on anxious, avoidant, and secure attachment makes sense, it left out other styles and nuances that exist within the spectrum. human behaviour isn’t always that neatly categorized, and i found myself wishing it had gone a little deeper into those complexities. overall, attached is a fantastic starting point if you want to book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: A friend of mine suggested this to me a few weeks ago, as one of the best relationship books she's read, and it is one of the books I've come across in the self-help/psychology/relationship category. Truthfully, I wish I had this book years ago, but, as the saying goes, when the student is ready the teacher appears...And the right books get put on our bookshelves at the right times. It basically covers our individual attachment styles (Secure, Anxious, Avoidant) and how we can better recognize our attachment types, as well as those of our partners, and offers a lot of case studies on how to improve our interactions with partners through more effective communications. This will be a re-read shortly, as there is just an amazing amount of information to absorb, even though the book is not lengthy, and is written is a user-friendly style. The book concludes with the author's sharing insights into a romantic comedy, where they both, even though empowered by years of study in attachment theory, fell prey to wanting the lead characters to fall into 'happy ever after land'. The movie sounds a lot like '(500) Days of Summer', which made the story even more amusing...I picked Zooey Deschanel's character out to being someone who would leave the guy (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) in ruins from square one. :)

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: how come no one told me before? codependency doesn't exist...or at least is overblown "problem" in the self-help marketplace. it is a natural and biological response to be dependent on an intimate partner or caregiver, so of course we will be impacted by the actions, absence, etc of others. that's OKAY! wow! another (along with Wired for Love) validating and positive look at the potential for relationships to offer us support, understanding, and healing in a way our primary caretakers didn't--not because we have to, but because we want to, our lives are enhanced by giving and receiving love! hooray! whatever behaviors i had previously labeled as "codependent" or pathologized were simply having my need for intimacy and desire for closeness devalued, insulted, and pushed away by people for whom intimacy is uncomfortable. my acting out or internalizing shame was due to attributing someone's lack of interest in intimacy with me as something being wrong with me rather than as their attachment style--they don't like intimacy with anyone, and particularly not the kind of intimacy, that i, as anxiously attached individual, want...so another book that advocates for an anxious-secure pairing...what a difference it makes. hallelujah!

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I often feel like I become a completely different person when I get into relationships, usually I am independent, self sufficient, light and easy but I get super intense, needy, self conscious and become easily consumed by the person I am dating. I always wonder why even assume I might have low self esteem or I just have a lot of unhealed trauma that creeps up when I get in relationships. I stumbled on this book on someone's Instagrams stories and decided to humor myself as I am always mad skeptical of anything self help or non fiction in general. I feel like it was the best decision I made. I have been able to understand myself so much and see every single situation I've been on romantically and why it never worked. I saw my attachment style always leading me negatively because once activated, I would always use protest habits to try and get my partners attention which would further draw them away. I feel like someone submerged me in knowledge and I am coming out with better and more self aware armed with effective communication skills and ability to use my attachment style to work for me in future relationships and not against. I have made so many notes and I am pretty sure I'll be coming back to this book again.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Upon starting all the way up to the finish I could see both what Levine and Keller were going for but also certain aspects/traits this book seems to lean in that might put off or not vibe with a certain reader, but for me I thought aside from being a bit slow I had a great time and learned quick a bit. I kind of knew going into this that I’d probably be an anxious attachment style (which I am) but truly aside from that blanket point and the brief synopsis, I had no idea what I was going into. This book seems to be both the go to source and also a diving off point for exploring and discovering the world of attachments styles in the greater whole world at large, with its biggest detractor by far being its lengthy monologue like nature at times that was full of useful but sadly too overly abundant amount of info that I found myself more than once needing to stop and reread a page or two. I’ve really enjoyed this recent explorative journey both for my internal as well as external person and to try to constantly evolve and be a better partner and parent and this gave a lot of helpful tips and opened some intriguing thought doors that I’ll be sure to look deeper into in some future books on the subject as well. 3.75/5

review_body: I had been thinking about adult attachment style s for some time and noted my friend Paresh reading this. I thought it would be worthwhile reading as I had come to the conclusion that attachment styles do not stop in your childhood and are the basis for a lot of the struggles we have in relationships when we get older. When I formerly answered the Mental Health Crisis Line, colleagues and I would often comment to each other ‘s/he is not mentally unwell, they just married the wrong person’. Two otherwise decent people, if incompatible, can combine to make each others lives hell. Levine and Heller are onto something when writing about adult attachment styles in intimate relationships worth contemplating. The book caused me to reflect on my own attachment style and I was definitely the anxious type. I cringe at the neediness I displayed in early relationships, as I waited for each girl to discover how awful I was and leave me. It was the honest recognition of a false belief of my worth as a person and became a self fulfilling prophecy. My ego was fragile and I was desperate to hide behind false bravado. Finding the right person is as important as the skills you can develop. According to the writers attachment styles are malleable and plastic. You can work on your own attachment style moving from anxious or avoidant to secure and vice versa. It requires a meta-awareness and willingness to work with unhelpful communication styles and maintenance of boundaries. Nothing beats becoming intimate with someone who you are compatible with. review_body: Attached boasts that it will explain how “the new science of adult attachment” can help you “find – and keep – love”. As someone who came into this book already familiar with attachment theory, I was interested to see how much of its contents would be reflective of academic orthodoxy and how much of it would be pop psychology fluff. I calculate the division around 75/25. The bedrock idea of attachment theory is that a combination of genetics, environment, early childhood experiences, and significant lifetime events place individuals on a spectrum of attachment between poles of ‘secure’ and ‘insecure’, with insecure styles being divided into two significant subtypes, ‘anxious’ and ‘avoidant’. Generally speaking, a person’s behaviors and attitudes in intimate relationships follow patterns associated with one of these three styles. As with most psychological jargon, it’s important to remember that these labels are descriptive, not prescriptive, and that most people fall along the vast distance between the two extremes. This is not controversial, nor is it especially “new”, per se. In the opening chapters of the book, the authors discuss the history of attachment theory, which was first formulated in the dwindling years of the second world war. So the title is a little bombastic, but we can forgive that in the name of good optics. The real meat of this book is in describing the three attachment styles, assisting individuals in determining theirs or their partners attachment style, and then providing a lengthy set of explanations for seemingly confusing and destructive behavior as well as a toolkit of strategies that can be used to be more sensitive to the needs of the partner with a divergent attachment style. review_body: A friend recommended this book to me after a discussion about how complicated all human relationships are, and I found it quite interesting! The premise of this is that there are, in general, three types of attachment that people might have: secure, anxious, and/or avoidant. Much research has been done about children being attached to their parents, but the authors of this book took those general ideas and applied it to adults and how an individual's attachment style impacts, helps, and/or exacerbates problems in a relationship. While much of this book seemed fairly simplistic and semi-obvious, it was presented in a really clear way that made for a lot of good pondering. This wasn't about how to change your style and become more secure, which I liked, but instead of recognizing what might be driving your attachment issues and responding to them in a better way for healthier, more positive, interactions with others. Many of the suggestions in here seemed to go against the typical dating advice you hear, which is basically about playing games with each other; instead, this stressed effective communication and being upfront (especially with yourself) about your attachment style in order to better understand what is going on and why you're feeling or acting a certain way. The advice in here also seemed to go against much of what seems to be commonly expected or encouraged in life - for example, being independent (good to a point, but they note that humans who feel like they can securely depend on someone else are happier and more confident because they're not stressed about their secure base). Maybe this isn't a groundbreaking or perfect book, but it was certainly an interesting take on what makes people act the way they do and how to better recognize and communicate issues in order to feel happier overall. review_body: Misleading to some extent. The book would've been a 4* as it offers good insights into the psychology of human connection. But some advice and statements are too generalised and one-dimensional, making it misleading if you're not actively on the lookout. "Today’s experts offer advice that goes something like this: Your happiness is something that should come from within and should not be dependent on your lover or mate. Each person needs to look after himself or herself. If you develop a strong dependency on your partner, you are deficient in some way. The worst possible scenario is that you will end up needing your partner, which is equated with “addiction” to him or her, and addiction, we all know, is a dangerous prospect." None of these statements are innately wrong. The book's intent isn't to bash on them (which it inadvertently does), but to point out the flaws in these schools of thoughts, where some adopt them as absolute ideals. There's a larger side of the picture, with much gray area. But the book doesn't cover these gray areas, it just goes on talking about how these ideas are straight up wrong . Things like this are highly misleading. For the most part, the book tells you what you want to hear. It's easy to jump to conclusions if you don't really give it much thought. It provides science and logic behind why we experience certain sets of emotions and act them out, and goes on to say they're only natural. But some blame goes to the people involved too; not all their emotions and needs are justified or good. The book doesn't address taking this accountability for yourself whatsoever. It also doesn't advice to judge yourself, and figure out where you're actually at fault. Questionable advice aside, there's a good bunch of psychology science in the book, and I got to learn a lot of new things from it. If you approach the book with the intent of salvaging the things you can, it can be a worthwhile read.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: In Attached , Amir Levine and Rachel S.F. Heller outline attachment theory and how it manifests in romantic relationships between adults. Levine and Heller outline several attachment tendencies, which are secure, anxious, avoidant, and anxious-avoidant. It seems likely that some form of this model must be correct, though I suppose a book like this is the last place to find out just how "real" this theory is or whether it has survived the replication crisis. Perhaps the most interesting insight in the book, aside from the attachments themselves, is that secures will partner up, thus leaving the dating market. It's not that one dates broken-hearted people as one ages so much as that mostly anxious and avoidants remain. If I were to push back on any insight, I'd interpret avoidants like this: they not only feel emotions the same as others but more likely feel them more strongly than others, so much so that they suppress attachments to protect against pain. Two criticisms... First, I find in these books much of the material can be learned without the book--just find some clickbait website or video. But if one wants to do a deep dive into the material, it's probably better to engage a therapist or a friend in conversation than to closely read Attached . Second, I suspect these tendencies are either genetic or imprinted in one's youth. Either way, I'm not sure how much control one can gain over them. It is almost cliche for therapists to advise people to talk clearly, as Levine and Heller do here, and yet I find people will just as likely move from one trap to a meta-form of it like this: -P1: B/c I'm anxious about our attachment, I'd appreciate if you texted me back constantly. -P2: You only want me to text you constantly b/c you're anxious about our attachment. Be reasonable. But if you've never heard of these theories, I'd certainly recommend this book to you. To contextualize it, I think its advice is better than what one gets in Five Love Languages . book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Pretty much changed my life. I had heard of the different types of attachments in the past but hadn’t paid much attention to them or to what they actually meant. But that’s all changed. I read this in less than 24 hours, on the whim, because I wanted to know more about myself and how others interact with me. For the first time, I think in a very long time, I didn’t feel ashamed of the needs I’ve always known I had. Society and avoidant partners would make people believe that your needs are clingy or undesirable but thats simply not true!! They’re your needs!!! If that doesn’t suit someone thats fine; find the next person who will. I really think this book can do wonders for the person who knows they need to read this. Seriously, cannot stop thinking about the dependency paradox and the loops anxious and avoidant partners fall into. This book will and already is a lifeline for me. All the pages are highlighted to the brim. All its sentences in my head. Seriously mind altering. Even if someone disagrees with any major premise in this book, I’m sure anybody can read this and gain at least one new thing to practice in their relationships. Be it effective communication, more consideration, etc. Can’t say it isn’t depressing at times, it makes you realise a lot… lot, of things, but in the end it’s for the better. It’s really weird to look at past relationships, fictional relationships, my friends’ relationships etc and kind of realise the root problem of them all. Even weirder to see the dating advice going around, especially on the internet that encourages mind games and everything else that involves silencing yourself all in the name of getting one silly person to like you. Friends!!! It’s time to stop thinking that you need to get them to like you and do everything you can to keep them around. Instead ask yourself if they can effectively meet YOUR needs and love you the way you need them too! Definitely never going to forget this book.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Although some of the ideas and concepts broached in this work definitely merit some consideration, and there are no doubt some quite pertinent lessons to be taken away, as a whole it isn't what I was expecting - which is largely on me. I came into the work expecting a semi pop-psychology, relatively neutral exploration of academic studies, not a how-to guidebook. I feel as though certain situations are excessively simplified and overdone, almost so I feel as though the work is pushing an agenda of sorts as it attempts to cram its ideas down my throat repeatedly. Some key points - studies were only conducted in Western, industrialised and modern societies so im curious about how true its concepts are when applied to the rest of the world. Blanketing all needs as neutral and neither good or bad is, in my opinion harmful, or at least can be harmful. It does feel as though much of the novel is largely about expressing your own individualistic needs and wants, rather than attempting to grow as an individual and improve oneself. I.e, finding someone who loves you as you are, instead of actively also taking steps to build upon your weaknesses and personal biases or traumas. Although I recognise the idea, I am hesitant as it feels as though it almost excuses inaction or justifies needs that are unhealthy. Interesting tidbits - happiness is only real when it is shared - the joy of being part of something larger than yourself - using your relationships with your pets as a secure role model - the danger of too much parental love and affection - After all, we live in a culture that seems to scorn basic needs for intimacy, closeness, and especially dependency, while exalting independence - dependency Paradox All in all, an interesting, albeit laborious read. I don't feel as I gained much past the description and exploration of the attachment types, but there were some fresh perspectives, so that's nice. Perhaps a bit more nuance and objective viewpoint would have been better for

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: És increïble com un pot pensar que està sol en certes experiències i després descobrir que no, que moltes coses tenen una explicació científica, o sociològica, i que són patrons apresos o desenvolupats a base d'experiències passades, compartides per molta gent d'aquest món. La informació que es dona en aquest llibre és, al meu entendre, d'un valor incalculable. Entendre les relacions sota la ciència de la vinculació, sota la ciència de l'"apego adulto", ajuda a comprendre enormement a un mateix i als altres. És increïble el poc que ens ensenyen a l'escola a gestionar-nos, a veure més enllà, a cultivar l'empatia i la sensibilitat per tal de poder entendre millor a l'altre i connectar-se de manera més segura. Aquesta nova branca de l'estudi de les relacions es basa en la creença que hi ha tres tipus de vinculació: l'ansiosa, l'evitativa i la segura. Recomano molt aquest llibre si correspons a un dels dos primers tipus de vinculacions, o si tens dubtes sobre a quin tipus pertanys. El llibre t'explica de manera molt clara la diferència, les trampes o les dificultats que et pots trobar si et vincules amb un o altre, sent tu X o Y, i de quina manera podem aprendre de la gent segura. M'agrada com aquest llibre trenca tabús i advoca per una comunicació eficient i una acceptació de les necessitats d'intimitat de cadascú. Ens hem de conèixer i ens hem d'estimar, en especial els ansiosos, als qui la societat té tant trinxats. També m'agrada l'èmfasi que posa el llibre en la plasticitat del tipus "d'apego". Un ansiós i un evitatiu poden passar a ser segurs si es coneixen i es treballen i, a poc a poc, eduquen el cervell perquè així ho sigui. Es tracta de conèixer les alternatives, conèixer eines de resolució de conflictes i de comunicació eficient. Si actues com un segur, encara que et resulti antinatural al principi, al final ho acabaràs sent (tot i les teves tendències que, per descomptat, sempre hi seran i hem d'acceptar i respectar). book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I read Attached at the recommendation of my therapist, who quickly identified that both my boyfriend and I had anxious attachment styles. For the first couple hours, I found this book helpful. It explains how the attachment styles work, the science behind the hypothesis, how to identify each style, and your ideal match based on your type. And then it goes on. And on. And on. And on. And on. And on. The repetition killed me. This book could have been about a quarter to a third of its actual length and I would have gotten just as much information out of it. I think the repetition was in part because the author legitimately didn’t expect people to read the full book, which is kind of sad. He kept saying things like “in chapter 8 we will go over this more” and I’d think of how much of my time he was wasting mentioning this repeatedly, as I’d hear it when I actually got to chapter 8. I love to read and learn, but I was honestly bored out of my mind by the end of the book. Also, considering how long it droned on about things that were obvious, it could have covered one of the few topics I cared about, which is what to do when two anxious people are in a relationship. I don’t think it was mentioned once. We hear repeatedly how anxious people should be with secure people and not avoidant people. We hear how avoidant people should also date secure people and how relationships between avoidant people hardly ever happen because they avoid each other over time. How was an anxious-anxious pairing not mentioned at all? Overall, I genuinely think that Attached was helpful in identifying the attachment styles of both myself and my partner. I learned more about the ways in which we respond to stress, but not how our anxiety over the relationship impacts one another. The hypothesis makes genuine sense and it’s easy to apply it to TV characters and such as practice for identifying people in the real world. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I give this 4 starts because overall I did find the 'attachment theory' lens useful and applicable, and this book was an interesting listen. I only wish I had read this book when I was 19 and not 33, lol. But it is still useful now in making sense of past relationships and in trying to develop into a better partner now. However, the book is also extremely repetitive in trying to drive the point home. It could have easily been a lot shorter and still conveyed all the same ideas. Also, it seemed to almost exclusively focus on cis-het couples (I think there was one mention of a gay couple) and usually portrayed the 'avoidant' types as a man and the 'insecure' types as a woman. Also, it kind of implies that attachment style is the 'be-all end-all' of compatibility and that you should latch on to any 'secure attachment' person you can find, but of course you still would take personality, interests, and attraction into account. I think it would be interesting to release a revised edition of this book that takes a more multi-layered approach in analyzing how different attachment styles might interact with different (basic) personality types. For example, an extroverted avoidant person might have different tendencies than an introverted avoidant person. But also, that stuff might be too subjective to dive into. edit: After reading Melody's review on Goodreads from 2017 (top review on the book page) I do agree with about everything she said. The book is heavily biased in supporting the 'anxious' attachment types but I can see how, if you identify as 'secure,' this book not very useful, and if you identify as 'avoidant' you may feel you are being portrayed as a villain. The book could have handled the 'avoidant' type with a lot more nuance and support. It reads more like a manual for 'anxious' types.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book was very enlightning for me and actually made me deeply reflect on how I've approached my past dating experiences. As someone who is healing from an insecure attachement, this book made me realize not only some of my behaviour patterns, but also it validated my healing process, describing the methods to become more secure that I've learned through the past years. "Turn offs" about this book are: the absence of inclusive language and LGBTQIA+ representation in the examples (why didn't the authors use simply they/them pronouns, instead of always repeating s/he or "himself or herself"? it is not only the most inclusive and correct solution, but also the quickest one!), the sort of villanization of the avoidant partner - I felt like the book focused more on teaching anxious attached people to avoid avoidant people and how to become more secure, rather than teaching how to overcome and heal from your insecure attachement, also for avoidant people (I also think they portraited a very negative image of avoidant people, even if they are, exactly like anxious people, victims of the attachement they developed-, and finally, I feel that love is so much more than a romantic relationship, and this book only took into consideration cases of people who are in a couple or have been. Even if the book focused on romantic love and relationships, I did find many resemblances between the given examples and other kinds of relationships with loved ones that I personally experiences. Effective communication is in fact not only essential to practise with a partner/or partners, but also in all of our social interactions, and insecure or secure attachments do manifest in all of our relationships. Still, the authors' approach was also very interesting as an education and psychology student.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Ooook, new to reviews here but I feel quite affected. More than quite actually. In particular, as someone who (unfortunately) recognise himself fitting 99.9% the avoidant type, I could not avoid a strong sense of guilt while reading this book, especially considering the phase of life I am going through. I could recognise so many of the negative traits that are part of me and as often happens when I explore such topic, it does scare me. Is that supposed to be what this book aims for? I like to believe differently. It has clearly some valid discussion points, but to me the issue lays with the attempt of trying to explain rationally something irrational. The book makes you feel like love is a numbers game, and maybe some people do believe that. You go out there in the world, date date and date until you find the right person. This does not resonate with me. I like to believe love is something different. Yes, compatibility might be a huge factor, but what does not say is that feelings go beyond what is right or wrong. We fall in love in mysterious ways. Sometimes with who they call the “wrong” person in this book. But who says wrong? Far too often we look at our partner and their attachment style but is not much harder to look at ourselves instead? So that we allow our partner to feel vulnerable with us. So that we become the right person. Love has no rules, so try to take this book as a guide to work towards your partner but especially to the best version of yourself, understand the challenges of your attachment style, accept them and try to work on those. You will get to the point you want to do something about your attachment issues. Is it really about the right person? Maybe that person is just right for you but you’re not in the right place. If you love someone, then try hard to make it work, don’t look somewhere else with the idea of I’ll find the “one”, because you need to be the right one first. Don’t be fearful of sharing your emotions.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I really enjoyed reading attached. Many reviews mention that the authors focused on the anxious attachment style, more so than the avoidant attachment style and I personally disagree. As someone who waxes and wanes between both due to my anxious-avoidant attachment style, I felt that the authors discussed the 3 attachment styles in an equal manner. This book serves as an introductory guide to attachment styles. Generally, the premise of the book seems to guide readers to identify their attachment style, as well as to identify the attachment style of others. With that being said, if you are looking for an in-depth analysis of your attachment style, this book will not satisfy you. The book includes prompts to guide self-reflection and provides stories in real time to demonstrate the tendencies and behaviours of each attachment style. There is a chapter dedicated to each style, which explores the attitudes, behaviours and defense mechanisms unique to each style. The anxiously attached seeks intimacy and engages in activation strategies and protest behaviours, as a result of not receiving the desired intimacy. In contrast, the avoidant attachment style seeks distance and engages in deactivation strategies, to repress their needs for intimacy. Both insecure attachment styles will be examined and given secure principles to develop healthy relationships. Again, this book offers introductory information for each attachment style. It covers the characteristics of each style, how to identity them and guides readers toward the development of a secure attachment. I do believe that the authors could have provided more insight about childhood attachment and how parenting styles influence our adult attachment. However, attachment research is vast and the purpose of the book seems to provide introductory information. The book also lacks lgbtq+ representation but the author included a note about this in their foreword. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this book and learnt a great deal

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I picked this title up with the intention of learning more about modern attachment science. While the concepts herein are rooted in research, the conclusions drawn by the authors amount to generic relationship help at best, deeply problematic at worst. Right away, while giving a basic overview of the attachment styles, the authors state that none of the types are inherently pathological - then proceed to pathologize the avoidant style throughout the entire rest of the book. While anxious styles' needs are consistently validated, those with avoidant styles are repeatedly portrayed in the given examples as emotionally stunted, abusive and narcissistic. Those more familiar with modern attachment will note the absence of a distinction between "fearful-avoidant" and "dismissive-avoidant". There's little to no discussion of the effects of trauma or emotional neglect on attachment styles; no acknowledgement that an individual may move from a secure childhood attachment to an insecure place as a result of life experiences, and virtually no advice for those with avoidant attachment styles who may have picked up the book in an honest effort to understand themselves and their partner and expand their relational toolkit. Sweeping generalizations without evidence are commonplace. There's plenty of questionable and tone-deaf advice given to those who identify as anxious, too. "Just date lots and lots of people; it should be no problem finding literally hundreds of people to date until you find the person who will take your codependency, jealousy and protest behaviors in stride". I'm sorry - what? Have you heard of some of the societal issues facing millennials in 2022? Crushing student loan debt, wage stagnation, inflation, rapidly rising rent and home costs? No? Oof. Just "date lots of people". Duh. *Facepalm*. In conclusion, I can understand the appeal of a book that channels attachment into quantifiable styles, but this book is grossly overhyped and not worth the investment in

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: While this book provided a pretty good introduction to attachment theory, I found that there was a little too much emphasis on finding the “right” partner and essentially avoiding those with an avoidant attachment style. Much of the book focused on the anxious-avoidant cycle, which is definitely important to be aware of. However, I would’ve liked to see more information about the relationship dynamics between two anxiously attached people. I found that the book didn’t really showcase this type of relationship at all, which is what I was truly hoping for from this book. I found that this book also placed a little too much emphasis on the importance of being with a secure partner, rather than providing tools for how to manage your own insecurities in relationships. Contrary to this book’s assertions, as an anxiously attached person, simply being with someone who is securely attached is not enough to relinquish one’s fears in relationships. In fact, sometimes securely attached people can activate anxiously attached people’s fears even more, by activating thoughts such as “if this person isn’t afraid to lose me, this must mean they don’t care about me.” The book didn’t really talk about this at all, which was disappointing. I also think that the way this book demonized avoidants was unnecessary and unfair. Not all avoidants are malicious, cold-hearted, and cruel. The book also didn’t talk at all about the anxious-avoidant attachment style, which was another let down. Overall, this book provides a decent background on attachment theory without going into much depth about the complexities of relationships between differing attachment styles (aside from relationships between anxious & avoidant people).

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: as someone who has experienced shifts in attachment styles depending on partners & context, i found attached to be overly simplistic & superficial. the book focuses predominantly on those with anxious attachment, offering them validation & strategies for seeking healthier relationships. it falls short when addressing the complexities of avoidant attachment, painting avoidant individuals as fundamentally different or emotionally unavailable without exploring further. while anxious individuals are encouraged to embrace their needs & avoid settling for partners who cannot meet them, avoidant individuals are told to make concessions to participate in relationships & framed as cold or toxic. this one-sided advice overlooks the fact that avoidants may have their own emotional needs & challenges in expressing love due to their past experiences & does little in ways of offering support or ways to improve. it is an imbalanced perspective that risks alienating readers who identity with avoidant behaviors & teaches others that avoidants are better off avoided than understood. it is very heteronormative & usually depicts women as anxious victims of unfeeling avoidant men who are incapable of meeting the needs of their partners. it also touches on codependency in a way that can be misleading. the authors critique codependent theory, advocating instead for interdependence in relationships. while this is valid, it lacks nuance. codependent behaviors can be harmful to the relationship as well as the individual, & the book does not address where the line between healthy interdependence and damaging codependency should be drawn. those looking for more balanced & inclusive perspectives on attachment styles will need to look elsewhere. ★★☆☆☆

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Tremendously informative and perspective broadening.. and a little bit annoying and depressing. The practical part is lost on those whom are not in a serious relationship, nevertheless, I think it is really helpful to have an idea that probably may implemented in the future. The need for attachment to someone is in our genes. A fundemental human need. Admitting this requires a revisit to our current view of dependence. Paradoxically, dependence is a prerequisite for independence. To be independent to navigate the world and be who you want to be you need to depend on another and be secure in that knowledge. Ok, attachement is a universal human need. But how we do attach is tricky. It comes about in three human forms: secure, anxious, and avoidant. The book covers each very well with many examples on how to identify your style and your other significant other or any one you're in a relationship with, and how to adress the insecure types' devastating effect on relationships. I liked the part on effective communication and the implicit idea throughout the book that marriage and relationships require effort, really effective communication, and compatibility; and not merely some crappy butterfly feeling many people consider love which is not, actually it is a warning sign that your insecure attachment is activated. When time comes, imma be memorizin' this one. (Forget about what I said earlier about the book being annoying and depressing.. it is just a recurrent temporal idiosyncratic reaction to most books on love and relationships.. can't help it! N, n, n, nno, I'm not an avoidant lol currently, judgment is suspended.)

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: As a therapist who works primarily from attachment and trauma theory and research, I was very interested in this book and wanted to see if it would be a good one to recommend to clients. On the whole, I would say yes I would recommend it but with caveats. It’s not a bad summary of attachment theory but it is, at times, a bit of an oversimplification. I do not think someone with insecure attachment is going to be able to read this book and walk away with the skills necessary to form secure attachments; that takes a ton of work and practice. Learning how to self soothe enough to be able to recognize and avoid protest behaviors is very, very hard work. I like that this book presents a clear message that attachment needs are not wrong or bad, and that you can change your attachment style. This is a hopeful and shame reducing message about attachment. However, I feel like it would be easy to take away from this book a message that if you have insecure attachment, your partner better be able to meet your needs or you should leave the relationship. This is simply not true or possible, though. Even a securely attached person will not be able to 100% meet the needs and wants of an insecurely attached person and they are going to have to learn to recognize when this is the case and self soothe at least some of the time. I don’t think this is the message the authors meant to convey, but I think some readers could get that message anyway. I also wish this book would have included more information about how and why attachment styles tend to fall on such gendered lines (I don’t even know that there is a lot of research on this, but my guess is we socialize boys to need/expect attachment less in order to fit societal standards of masculinity so they are more likely to be avoidant). Overall, the section of this book dedicated to explaining attachment was mostly good. book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: The book is all about attachment, exploring its significance and origins, and it contains knowledge that is applicable to everyone, so I would recommend it to anyone interested in exploring attachment. The author uses clear examples to illustrate the key concepts. Here are my takeaways from the book: Why attachment is important Having a strong attachment bond with someone provides a secure emotional foundation. This reduces stress and anxiety, and is essential for a healthy and happy life. Anxious attachment style People with an anxious attachment style crave intimacy and worry excessively about their relationships. They need a partner with a secure attachment style, who can provide emotional security and constant availability, to feel loved and understood. Avoidant attachment style People with an avoidant attachment style crave independence in relationships and fear losing autonomy, which leads them to maintain emotional distance and struggle with intimacy. In order to make relationships work, avoidants must learn to think positively about their partner, take responsibility for conflicts, and consider their partner's perspective. Secure attachment style People with a secure attachment style are comfortable with intimacy, can read their partner's needs, and are more likely to have a happy relationship. Having a secure partner can improve the quality of a relationship, even if the other partner has a different attachment style. This is because they understand and support each other's needs. The anxious-avoidant trap A dysfunctional relationship dynamic occurs when an anxious person, who craves intimacy, is paired with an avoidant person, who fears intimacy and needs independence. This creates a push-pull cycle where the anxious person seeks closeness, causing the avoidant person to pull away, leading to a never-ending cycle of approach and withdrawal.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: کتاب وابسته، بررسی عمیقی از تأثیر سبک‌های دلبستگی بر روابط عاشقانه ارائه می‌دهد. این کتاب افراد را به سه دسته دلبسته اضطرابی، اجتنابی و ایمن تقسیم می‌کند و توضیح می‌دهد که این سبک‌ها چگونه بر نحوه ارتباط ما با شریک عاطفی تأثیر می‌گذارند. یکی از نقاط قوت این کتاب، ساده‌سازی مفاهیم پیچیده روان‌شناسی به زبان عملی و قابل‌فهم است. نویسندگان با ارائه مثال‌های واقعی، آزمون‌های خودشناسی، و راهکارهای کاربردی، به خوانندگان کمک می‌کنند تا الگوهای رفتاری خود را بشناسند و تصمیمات بهتری بگیرند. آنها بر این نکته تأکید دارند که شناخت سبک دلبستگی به معنای برچسب زدن به افراد نیست، بلکه راهی برای افزایش آگاهی و بهبود روابط است. با این حال، این کتاب گاهی روابط انسانی را بیش از حد ساده‌سازی می‌کند. تعاملات واقعی پیچیده‌تر از سه دسته کلی هستند و تمرکز کتاب تقریباً به‌طور کامل بر روابط عاشقانه است، بدون بررسی تأثیر دلبستگی در دوستی‌ها یا روابط خانوادگی. همچنین، برخی توصیه‌ها ممکن است برای همه افراد کاربرد نداشته باشد. به‌طور کلی، وابسته کتابی ارزشمند برای افرادی است که می‌خواهند روابط عاشقانه خود را بهتر درک کنند. این کتاب پایه‌ای قوی برای خودآگاهی و رشد شخصی فراهم می‌کند، هرچند که ممکن است برای درک جامع‌تر، نیاز به مطالعه منابع تکمیلی باشد *People with an anxious attachment style are often preoccupied with their relationships and tend to worry about their partner’s ability to love them back. They are highly sensitive to their partner’s moods and actions, sometimes interpreting them as signs of rejection, even when no rejection is intended. *People with an avoidant attachment style value their independence and self-sufficiency. They often equate intimacy with a loss of freedom and may become uncomfortable when a relationship gets too close.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I went to the book store one day, when I felt like I could not take this feeling anymore. I’m in a difficult yet crucial stage of my life when it comes to love and relationships, so in an attempt to better understand myself I bought this book. Coming into “Attached”, my understanding was that attachment theory is some kind of pseudoscience. Afterwards, I’m not so sure, and I’m also not sure I like what it tells me about myself. The authors take distance from today’s misconceptions such as “you should not emotionally depend on your partner” and “fights do not occur in healthy relationships”. Turns out, we are biologically programmed to depend on another. Codependency was a great means to ensure survival and procreation, and that is supposedly why we grow attached to people. But humans thrived in many different conditions, and some favoured different levels of attachment. Hence the three types: anxious, avoidant, and secure. The book reserves a lot of its pages to discuss the seemingly all too common “anxious-avoidant trap”, where an anxious person pursues an avoidant one in an increasingly painful dance of attachment styles. Contrary to popular belief, and what I have personally been brought up with, the authors argue that we can’t find proper love with anyone *just because we’re in love with them*. When you have your rose tinted shades equipped, that is when you should take a step back and analyse the person you have fallen for. Is this someone who can give me what I need? If not, force yourself to stop pursuing them because proper love is all too precious a thing to be missing out on. It is my hope and belief that I am now slightly better equipped to navigate life and move towards my end goal of a strong and loving relationship.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Insightful read, however I would strongly recommend interpreting this as more of a study of attachment behaviors and taking it as insight into dating and relationships and how past experiences, whether good or bad, can affect your dating experience rather than a sure and solid solution to finding love. In other words: This book is a tool, not an answer. I've carefully read a lot of reviews from other readers that generally say it's insightful but is lacking in scope for people of other attachment styles or it paints some as entirely bad/toxic. I strongly agree that it could've used a wider scope going into the topic, but I don't think they intended to paint any particular style as purely bad or toxic. To me it feels they were trying to point out toxic behaviors that are a common byproduct of miscommunication mingled with these styles as a sort of guide. At worst, it's too small of a scope for such a complex topic and it may come off as one-sided and maybe pandering to those with anxious attachment styles, but I would still recommend as it could spark some intense self reflection! However, I urge people to be cognizant of other variables to the behaviors and attachment styles mentioned such as past experiences, trauma, etc (which I think this could have delved much deeper into). These are just my thoughts and I truly do admire the effort of this book and the opinions of other readers. Dating is incredibly tedious and complicated and I believe the key in navigating this maze is looking inward!

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Uma leitura bastante informativa sobre os estilos de vinculação. Os únicos pontos negativos que tenho a apontar é que, como referiram outros comentários, foi um bocado parcial em relação ao estilo ansioso (parecia ter uma subconscious bias contra o estilo evitante) e praticamente não mencionou o estilo fearful avoidant. Algumas coisas úteis que retirei deste livro: - As nossas necessidades emocionais são válidas/legítimas e não temos de sentir vergonha delas. Não são boas nem más, mas são necessárias para o nosso bem-estar; - É inevitável sentirmo-nos um pouco dependentes da pessoa com quem estamos, porque passados a formar uma unidade emocional (é literalmente algo biológico, por ex., stress na relação pode influenciar a nossa pressão arterial), e não temos de nos sentir mal por isso. Pessoas com um estilo de vinculação seguro geralmente encaram o bem-estar da pessoa com quem estão como responsabilidade sua também; - É importante comunicar diretamente o que nos incomoda em vez de recorrer a comportamentos de protesto. Mesmo que a outra pessoa reaja negativamente, sabemos que está a reagir à nossa necessidade e não ao comportamento em si; - Num conflito, é importante não perder de vista o bem-estar da pessoa com quem estamos, mesmo que discordemos dela; - Receber mensagens ambivalentes de outra pessoa (geralmente, um evitante) pode tornar-se bastante viciante, mas não quer dizer que estejamos verdadeiramente apaixonados; apenas quer dizer que o nosso estilo de vinculação está ativado, ao ponto de só nos conseguirmos focar na outra pessoa e no próximo momento em que ela nos vai (ou não) dar atenção.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I’d heard a lot about this book and was excited to read it and learn more about attachment theory. While I think there’s some merit in this book, overall it fell short. It read more as an introductory to attachment theory rather than a deep dive into the topic. I found it disappointing and lacking. A lot of the examples given in the book felt pretty extreme with most exhibiting either very strong anxious or avoidant tendencies. The attachment styles felt so strong/blatant that rather than it seeming realistic, it felt more like textbook examples of insecure attachment. It didn’t get into the subtleties of the attachments, and instead covered broad brushstrokes of each. Again - felt more like an introduction to the topic rather than a thorough analysis. The book felt very biased. A lot of empathy was given to those with anxious attachment, praise to those with secure attachment, and it painted out those with avoidant attachment to be cold, unloving, and selfish. Given that both anxious and avoidant attachments are insecure attachments, I would have liked there to be more empathy to both sides - rather than painting avoidant attachments out as cold and anxious attachments out as victims of the avoidant. In addition to the bias, the main part of the book seemed to be offering tools and guidance largely/primarily to those with anxious attachment styles - it didn’t seem to be a well rounded analysis or offer advice to all the styles equally. If you’ve never heard of attachment theory, this is possibly worth reading - but if you’re familiar with it, you will likely not gain much from it.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Honestly, this is a life changing book. I couldn’t put it down and read it in one day. Learning more about my attachment style and the factors that contribute to it; recognizing my tendencies and the factors and motivations behind them; learning to recognize and identify insecure and secure attachment habits will change my life and my relationships. For those with few secure relationships that model healthy attachment styles, this book is a godsend. Major takeaways for me: - Theway we attach (secure, anxious, or avoidant) has evolutionary roots. It is better to understand these instincts and learn how to work w them rather than beat ourselves or others up about them - We are wired for connection and dependency. No matter how independent we are or want to be, connection is part of our evolutionary nature. We form physiological bonds w our attachment figures so who we attach to matters. Choose partners or loved ones who will help nurture you physiologically. “Attachment principles teach us that most people are only as needy as their unmet needs.” “In a true partnership, both partners view it as their responsibility to ensure the other’s emotional well-being.” “Getting attached means that our brain becomes wired to seek the support of our partner by ensuring the partner’s psychological and physical proximity.” “Avoidant people equate intimacy with a loss of independence and constantly try to minimize closeness.” “These findings suggest that people with an anxious attachment style are indeed more vigilant to changes in others’ emotional expression and can have a higher degree of accuracy and sensitivity to other people’s cues. However, this finding comes with a caveat. The study showed that people with an anxious attachment style tend to jump to conclusions very quickly, and when they do, they tend to misinterpret people’s emotional state.... If you just wait a little longer before reacting and jumping to conclusions, you will have an uncanny ability to decipher the wor

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Me ha gustado mucho el libro, y me ha ayudado a profundizar en el sistema de apego, ya que desde la carrera de Psicología solo lo enfocan desde la perspectiva de las figuras de apego primarias. Me ha ayudado a entender las necesidades, las reacciones y los bucles de cada uno de los sistemas de apego dentro de las relaciones de pareja, y me parece bastante útil a nivel, tanto personal como profesional. Dentro de las cosas que no me han gustado es que hay una fina línea entre interpretar tener apego evitativo y algunas formas de maltrato. En el capítulo 10, el caso de Marsha y Craig es un ejemplo: el libro lo analiza desde el prisma que es una relación dónde ambos miembros tienen sistema de apego incompatibles (ansiosa-evitativo) y llega un punto que esto es insostenible y es mejor que esta relación finalice. No obstante, se interpreta las reacciones de Craig como estrategias de desactivación del apego evitativo cuando, a mi parecer, son formas de maltrato psicológico puro y duro. También, creo que a veces es difícil etiquetar de forma rígida a alguien con un estilo de apego. En mi caso, me salió apego seguro pero tenía también rasgos del apego ansioso y, en menor medida, del evitativo, por lo que encasillarte en uno creo que no siempre es lo correcto. Igualmente, el libro me ha parecido muy útil y me ha ayudado a profundizar en el tema. Se hace muy ameno con la cantidad de ejemplos de casos y ejercicios autoaplicables. Posiblemente, me lea algunos capítulos de nuevo 😊

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I'm the type of person who gives 5 stars for everything in every feedback form at a restaurant or a customer service call. (I'd rather give stars than money. Joking. I'm pretty lenient, especially when someone's wage depends on my humble opinion.) Then I read somewhere that an average human can only read a few hundred books in their lifetime. With social media, visual entertainment, and several other things to keep us occupied, perhaps even less than a hundred really good books in a lifetime. That's a life-changing thought. It made me rethink several things. From using social media to feed people useless content about my burned dosa to the availability of blogging platforms making a poor writer out of us, to the several rubbish books I read because it was free on Kindle. So, I've decided that one has to be more thoughtful about giving stars to books since we've concluded to only read a few hundred books in a lifetime, it has to be somewhat telling if I gave a book five stars. A four-star book, in my opinion, is one that significantly changed what I think or had huge takeaways from. A five-star book is one that both significantly changed how I think and I also recommend others to read it. It has to be one of those few hundred books you read in your lifetime. Attached by Amir Levine is one five-star book I read recently. It touches the tip of the iceberg that is attachment theory, of which I wish I had learned about sooner. It tells that attachment is normal, it's doesn't deserve a perverse connotation as "clingy". We, humans, are all only as attached as our unmet needs. Which means we are not clingy if our attachment needs are met. There are broadly four kinds of attachment styles and not all types fit each other. Knowing what type other people are, can help us have a fair idea of whether or not our attachment needs will be met by them. It normalizes the need for attachment. The more effectively dependent people are on one another, the more independent and daring the

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I listened to it on Audible. I would say my perspective towards this was similar to when I would flip through Cosmo. A lot of generalizations in this book, but I still found it helpful in understanding some of my past relationships. Here are a few of my issues with it: A. It assumes that a person has predominantly one type of attachment style. I disagree with this. As a therapist and as, well, a human who has been in a fair number of relationships, I have displayed different attachment patterns at different points in my life and seen clients do the same. I am sure they would say that it is all insecure - I don't agree. B. The reason many women especially are avoidant is that many men don't get the point! Women are conditioned to not hurt others and that is more a socialization issue than an attachment issue. I do agree that effective communication is the way to go, though. C. Secure relationships also don't work out. Finding a secure mate does not guarantee a happily ever after. So putting secures on a pedestal is not enough. We gotta put in the work. All of us. Secures included. D. The book felt a bit dated because of largely heterosexual examples and a very Western lens. Ignores socio-cultural norms and brands everything as attachment. I would say approach it as a light read.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I have a lot of criticisms, but I didn’t hate this book. It felt… heteronormative. Specifically the word “mate” in reference to romantic partners. I don’t think they intended it to feel like that but it was vaguely irritating to listen to (audiobook). Also, it completely ignored nonstandard relationship styles and identities (polyamory, asexual, Demisexual, etc), which I find extremely irritating. Curious if they think that asexual people are actually just avoidant and using that as a tool? Or if demisexual people are avoidant until forming an emotional attachment and then become, what, secure? Anxious? Next point - trauma is completely unaddressed. Can a survivor of sexual violence have a secure relationship style but not have sex and emotional closeness inextricably linked? Or if you have trauma around sex does that mean you can never have a secure relationship style? Anyway. I’m not saying they’re wrong, obviously. I like the whole theory and I think it explains a LOT about a lot of people and unpacks a lot of relationship issues into pretty neat little boxes. But I do think they’re ignoring and invalidating a huge chunk of population that has non”standard” relationships or personal identities and I can’t tell if it’s a blind spot for the authors, or an intentional slight.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I think the chapters on Dependency (not a bad word) in the beginning and on Effective communication at the end contain the most important takeaways from this book. These topics could be be expanded into a whole book of their own. However, the rest of the book in between, discussing the 3 attachment styles (or really the 2 insecure attachment styles that this book is targeted at) can be quite reductive. I found myself going back and forth between the attachment style I identified with, and I'm still not very sure which one is correct. I understand that the text has to fit within the scope of the authors' research to remain scientific and factual, but I found the case studies described throughout Attached lacking a lot of the nuance that our real life relationships contain. By defining only 3 attachment styles This book restricts the full depth of relationship dynamics into broad archetypes. Perhaps it is good for readers to be aware of these archetypes; it can at least get you thinking about the challenges in your relationship and how to make steps to overcome them. But because of how rigid the definitions of each attachment style are, I think many readers could be misled into identifying with the wrong attachment style, or could be left uncertain about which style fits them. Although I do think it was beneficial to learn about the different behaviors associated with each attachment style, I believe that practicing effective communication is the best tool this books offers.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: The attachment theory categorizes people into secure, avoidant, and anxious attachment styles, and tells people to accept what they are and learn to communicate their needs. Unlike a lot of relationship advice that suggests everyone needs to be self-sufficient and not needy to be in love, this book argues that the partner should provide the emotional support that the other person needs. This is quite a refreshing view where the anxious people could benefit a lot from. However, the book does not offer useful advice for people who have other attachment styles. The avoidants often play the villain in the examples of this book; while the secures are the heroes that save the anxious people. I'd also like to see more discussion about how cultural background and gender affect a person's attachment style -- the book doesn't cover any of these, but I feel that people of different upbringings and genders have different distributions of attachment styles. So would I recommend this book? Yes, because it introduces an interesting theory and provides a new perspective. But do I think the arguments and generalizations in the book are all valid? Not really, I would suggest taking it as a grain as salt. People may show characteristics of particular attachment styles but don't behave the way as the book depicts, and thus don't benefit from the advices.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book has genuinely changed my life. I feel like this information has been in front of me for forever but I haven’t been able to make the connections I needed to make until this moment in time. That being said, I loved this book because I am the population it was written for—anxiously attached women. I do have some critiques, first being that the book mentions disorganized attachment maybe two times and then brushes over it for the rest of the book. It would have been a lot more helpful to have a chapter dedicated to it instead of just saying to read both anxious and avoidant chapters. The book also tends to vilify avoidant attachment and glorify secure attachment. To someone with an anxious attachment system, this is a pretty good working model of the kinds of people I should avoid or date in the future. But I can see it being a major turn off to anyone with an ounce of avoidance in their system. The book is also extremely heteronormative, with only one gay couple used as an example scenario. Where are the gays??? Where are the lesbians!!!! Overall, I thought this book was incredible (because it was written for me). Final thoughts: I am not needy for having needs; our biology has literally evolved to depend on a partner; effective communication only has a positive outcome.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Great overview of the 3 attachment types. I think I was expecting more depth, like where our tendencies to lean toward different attachment types originates. I feel like that would be worth at least acknowledging at some point in the book to provide further perspective on ourselves as readers. Nonetheless I think it’s still a solid read and if nothing else left me wanting to dive deeper which seems to meet the goal of this book! Would recommend to every person who intends to maintain even one relationship in their life. it’s an easy-to-understand, very quick read and provides super valuable insight into your attachment type - which in turn gives you perspective on behavior patterns (protest behavior/activating strategies) within relationships. Important stuff! Some bad reviews criticize that the book tends to focus on anxious attachment style. That is super curious to me because in learning about the avoidant attachment style (which is where I tend to lean) all avoidant is doing is using “deactivating strategies” to avoid being anxious - which becomes inevitable. For (a simplified) example, an avoidant May end a relationship because their partner was “clingy”. In separating from their partner the avoidant tends to fantasize their previous partner and begin to worry that they have messed everything up (anxious attachment) and even attempt to restart the relationship. Again I think this goes back to the overall mission of the book: to provide a simplified albeit surface level understanding of attachment styles and how to manage. I think what the bad review people are looking for is just more depth on the fundamental years and how that contributes to avoidant attachment styles. I’m not a psychologist though so what do I know 🤷🏽‍♂️

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Though I’ve not been one for a self-help novel previously, I found this book to be a strong primer on attachment theory and its utility in our romantic lives. There are definitely insightful nuggets throughout, and the included worksheets and “rules for the road” serve as good references to return to as needed. The book is certainly geared towards aiding anxiously attached individuals but does not leave much room for people with mixed or plastic attachment types. As anxious attachment is more overtly distressing, that focus is reasonable if incomplete and biased. It describes attachment as “stable and plastic,” meaning you can transition from an insecure (anxious OR avoidant) to a stable type with effort or with the help of a secure partner; however it does not sufficiently address people who have found themselves to be either form of insecurely attached in different relationships (or even in the same one at various time points!). Similarly, it isn’t that helpful in addressing deactivating/other strategies for people with avoidant tendencies. The included vignettes are mostly helpful if occasionally simplistic (and likely necessarily so for the purposes of a self help text). Overall, I think it’s worth a read for the process of self-examination of your actions in current/past relationships and the provided tools to grow as a better, more effectively communicative partner.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: There were some good takes from this book that I learnt, however, a fair amount I already knew. I listened to the audiobook of this and I really appreciated the PDF files attached to some of the chapters to be able to have access to do some work on it. However, it was a bit difficult to edit these files and I couldn’t find it available on my laptop but that’s likely a Spotify issue. It’s all easily accessible online anyway. Like what many other reviews say, it largely focuses on the anxious type and very much through their lens. I’m not a fan how the author tints a negative view on the avoidant type. It feels like the author is an anxious who was head over heels for an avoidant and from that breakup he focused on attachment types to help with his anxious attachments but still isn’t quite over his avoidant ex 🤣. It just felt pretty biased which shouldn’t be the case for this type of book. Also I know attachments are very much heightened and popularly focused in romantic relationships, however, I’d really like to see a book that focuses on attachments from all kinds of views as it can affect your platonic relationships, your daily life and your decisions through tough times etc… Somehow I can’t find a single book on that. This paragraph isn’t a review on this really… More of a rant and what would be great for psychologists like them to focus their research on.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: A really solid framework for looking at romantic relationships, but some critical issues. Didn’t love that the book didn’t define what love is (feels critical for the topic) and I felt what the author referred to as love is actually infatuation. bell hooks’ definition of love, continuously considering and prioritizing someone else’s growth, would void some of this author’s claims of couples in loving relationships. i.e. you can’t love someone if you are constantly hurting them, because that’s not what love is. But you may be infatuated by them This book mentions evolution several times and tries to imply that some things are innate or intended, but the author doesn’t use evolutionary theory correctly. This is may be expected from a casual thinker, but someone as academic as this author should have researched basics of evolutionary before making such claims. “Attached” also in my opinion undervalues non-romantic relationships and the importance of community in day-to-day life. Romantic relationships are often put on a pedestal, and while they are extremely important and impactful to most people, I think it is worth mentioning that they are not critical for a meaningful life. To take it a step further, even the most perfect romantic relationship is probably inadequate in meeting most people’s needs for community.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: After going through few first chapters I already knew that it will be a really worth read. After finishing it, I can honestly say that if I would have to pick three books that I am glad that I have read, this one would be among them. Attachment theory is nothing new but despite how much it can affect each one of us, I believe the concept is not that widely known. When I tried to dig deeper into it through the original works of John Bowlby, unfortunately the scientific language prevented me from doing so. This book filled in this gap by providing the reader with information about attachment theory, newest research on the subject which came since then and, what is most important, practical knowledge and examples on how exactly our attachment styles are influencing our relationships and what we can do about it. I would recommend this book to everyone, no matter their relationship history. Moreover, it will be exceptionally useful to you if in the past you have either noticed that you tend to distance yourself from the others or on the contrary you get attached quickly and you often find yourself trying to re-establish closeness with your partner. A truly great book packed with useful information and actionable advices. Strong recommendation :)

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: I liked this book. It's a good book, albeit a tad condescending. It's an important book for anyone undergoing character development. It emphasizes a very important point to make relationships work! Which is that dependency shouldn't be a bad word. And I agree, wholeheartedly. But the beginning of the book noted that there's no right or wrong attachment then later went on to praise one attachment style over the other two. Using it as a blueprint for all the other ones which are apparently wrong. 6 months ago, I would have felt very attacked by some of the habits that a certain attachment style tends to show in a relationship but I'm not that person anymore. Nowadays I gravitate towards healthy patterns of communication and conflict resolution. So this book to me was a reaffirmation that I really have grown over the past few months and it wasn't easy. Granted, I would have preferred the growth not being at someone's disadvantage but "if wishes were ponies then beggars would ride" as old adage goes. I also liked the important point that we shouldn't leave our relationship up to chance and hope they work out. We should strive to practice healthy patterns for our partners and ourselves if we want it to work.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: Caveat: I skimmed this book, only taking the assessments for myself and my partner and then reading the sections on the three attachment styles and effective communication. I'd recommend this book to anyone who wants to better understand attachment theory for adults and how to actually use it: its evolutionary ties, some common misconceptions (for example, that your adult attachment style is correlated with your child attachment style, or that non-secure styles are like disorders), and, most importantly, a high-level mental model for what is happening on a biological level when your attachment system is activated. This understanding helps me code my emotions as natural causes of my physiology, rather than faults of my personality (try to guess what attachment style I show). This is a valuable tool that I think will help strengthen my relationships in the future. My only complaint about this book is that it read a little prescriptive. While reading, I had to convince myself that attachment styles are styles rather than static attributes, and can change over time and based on the circumstances. The authors did mention this, but it felt like an addendum to what is first a guide to screening out bad potential matches for singles. Compatibility is more complex than matching attachment styles, especially for those of us that are already in relationships, so I wish that this was treated with more nuance or in a more up-front way.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
review_body: This book was fine? I appreciated some of the practical tips like being able to do an assessment/inventory and write down your needs and the issues in specific conflicts, but other than that I was a bit underwhelmed by this book. I think attachment theory IS really important and does help to understand a lot of things but the ways the authors explained it and made everything revolve around it made it seem a bit Myers Briggs-y in trying to put people into distinct categories and define their behaviour by that rather than acknowledging that many people can and do have big overlap between different styles (not to mention the authors are extremely dismissive of the Fearful avoidant style, which IS rare but they make it seem like it hardly exists and I think it’s around 5% of the population which is not insignificant). I felt like the authors really wanted attachment theory to explain everything and be this perfect key to solve all relationship issues and kinda sell it that way, but obviously that isn’t the case. Despite all this complaining, I do actually think there are some valuable things in this book and if you were just wanting a good first introduction to attachment styles I’m sure this would be a perfectly fine introduction. But I was personally craving more nuance, expansiveness and allowance for messiness. Not everything has to fit neatly in boxes.

book_title: Attached: The Science of Adult Attachment
